Page: Coding agents and MCP: grants and exit codes · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/developers/agents.html

# Agents and MCP
Coding agents need your keys to run tests and dev servers. With Pistachio they get them through pistachio run: the values reach the command, not the agent’s files, and you decide what an agent may use without asking.
## The pattern
- Keep references in env files: pistachio import .env.local --rewrite.
- Run anything that needs secrets through pistachio run.
- Decide what an agent may read without you: agent-safe items for values that aren’t secret, grants for a folder and a time. Everything else asks you, showing the agent’s process chain, folder and command.
Fresh git worktrees don’t have your .env (it’s gitignored). pistachio run --env PROJECT/ENV loads an environment’s items directly, and a grant for a repository’s folder covers its worktrees.
An agent runs its tests through pst run, and you allow the folder until the agent quits. Its next run goes through. A production item isn't covered, so it asks again, and a denial is exit 77. Example data; the output is what Pistachio prints.
## Skills and plugins
The Pistachio skill tells an agent to run commands through pst run, check before a slow run, never print or write a value, put references in env files, give you the pst set command for a missing key, suggest a session grant when you step away, and stop on 77 or 66.
- Claude Code: the plugin installs the skill and registers pst mcp as an MCP server. ~/.local/bin must be on the PATH Claude Code starts with.
- Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Cursor and other tools that read the Agent Skills format: copy the plugins/latchkey/skills/latchkey folder into the skills folder your tool reads, such as .agents/skills/ for Codex.
- Claude Desktop and other MCP clients without a shell: add pst mcp as a local MCP server. Chat apps that only reach MCP servers on the internet can’t use Pistachio, since its MCP server runs on your Mac.
Claude Code
```
/plugin install latchkey --marketplace zachshallbetter/latchkey
```
The repository is public, so the marketplace install should work, though it hasn’t been tried end to end yet. You can also add the plugin from a local checkout with /plugin marketplace add /path/to/pistachio.
## Instructions for agents
Without the skill, put this in CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md or your agent’s equivalent:
CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md
```
Secrets are in Pistachio. Env files hold pistachio:// references, not values.
Run anything that needs secrets as
`pistachio run --env-file .env.local -- <command>` or
`pistachio run --env <project>/<environment> -- <command>`.
Never run `pistachio get`, never print the environment, and never read or
write values in .env files. If pistachio exits with 77 (refused) or 66
(missing), stop and ask; don't retry.
```
## Exit codes to act on
CodeMeaningWhat an agent should do
0Done
64Wrong usageFix the command
66No item with that IDStop; ask the person to add it
69The Pistachio app can’t be reachedStop; ask the person to open Pistachio
73A file couldn’t be rewrittenStop and report
77Refused: not agent-safe, not approved, no grantStop; ask the person to approve or grant. Don’t retry
127The command couldn’t startFix the command
On 77 and 66 the message names the items and, for 77, the exact pistachio grant command that would allow them, for the person to run.
## Leaving an agent working
Terminal
```
pistachio grant 'shop/development/*' --session --for 4h                  # ends when the agent quits
pistachio grant 'shop/development/*' --command "npm test" --for 2h       # only this command
pistachio grant 'shop/development/*' --folder ~/Projects/shop --for 2h   # the folder, for a time
```
Run them inside the agent’s session (in Claude Code, start the line with !) so --session ties to the agent. The agent’s reads go through without asking until the grant ends, and each one is in the app’s Activity. End it early from Grants in the app or with pistachio revoke ID.
## Keys an agent can use but never read
For OpenAI and Anthropic keys, pistachio run --proxy (or proxy: true on pistachio_run) gives the command a placeholder and a local base URL, and adds the real key only to requests to the provider. An agent’s command can call the API but can’t print, encode or send the key anywhere else. See --proxy.
Only the command and the processes it starts can use the proxy; a request from any other program gets a 403, and the proxy stops when the command exits. To narrow what the command may do with the key, add --proxy-models A,B (only requests naming a listed model are forwarded) and --proxy-requests N (refuse requests after N). On pistachio_run these are proxy_models, an array of model names, and proxy_requests, a number; both need proxy: true. Pistachio says on standard error that the limits are enforced.
Terminal
```
pistachio run --proxy --proxy-models gpt-4o-mini --proxy-requests 100 --env shop/development -- npm test
```
## After an agent session
See what the agent was given, and replace anything you’d rather it no longer knew:
Terminal
```
pistachio touched --since 4h --by claude
pistachio rotate --touched --since 4h --by claude --open --push
```
## From another Mac over SSH
Forward Pistachio’s socket when you connect, then point pistachio on the other Mac at it:
Terminal
```
ssh -o StreamLocalBindUnlink=yes -R /tmp/pistachio-$USER.sock:"$HOME/Library/Application Support/Latchkey/broker.sock" devmac
```
On the other Mac
```
export PISTACHIO_SOCKET=/tmp/pistachio-$USER.sock
pistachio run --env shop/development -- npm test
```
$USER expands to your login name on each Mac: use the same name on both, or put a fixed name in both commands. Forwarding needs the direct-download app on your Mac; the Mac App Store version doesn’t support it yet, and if the other Mac has the App Store version installed, set PISTACHIO_BROKER=direct there.
- Each read that is not agent-safe asks. Your Mac sees only your ssh client, so grants don’t apply and can’t be made over the connection.
- The approval panel says so, and shows what the tool on the other computer says it’s running, marked as unchecked.
- The tool there can’t check the app’s signature through a forwarded socket; pistachio status says so.
- The other computer needs pistachio too; the tool is macOS only.
## Pistachio’s MCP server
pistachio mcp gives agents Pistachio’s tools over MCP: for clients without a shell, like Claude Desktop, and for structured refusals instead of exit codes. It has no direct secret-read tool. Child output masks exact secret values; transformed secrets can still leak.
Terminal
```
claude mcp add pistachio -- ~/.local/bin/pistachio mcp
```
Other clients
```
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "pistachio": { "command": "/Users/you/.local/bin/pistachio", "args": ["mcp"] }
  }
}
```
ToolWhat it doesAsks you?
pistachio_statusWhere values are kept, how you approve, item and grant countsNo
pistachio_listItem IDs with kind, service and agent-safe, by project or environment. Never valuesNo
pistachio_checkWhat a run would get without asking, what would ask, and what’s missing, for env_files, environments, files or idsNo
pistachio_runRuns command (an argument array) in cwd with references filled in. Returns the exit code and the output, masked. With proxy, proxy_models and proxy_requests limit what the command may do with the key (see above)When an item isn’t agent-safe or granted
pistachio_request_grantAsks you for a grant on ids in the agent’s folder for durationAlways
pistachio_projectWhich project the folder’s checkout is, from its Git remotes, and its environmentsNo
pistachio_export_referencesWrites an environment’s env file of references and plain settings, never values, inside its cwd onlyNo
- Output is always masked, and only the last 64 KB of each stream is returned, with a flag when it was cut. Standard input is empty.
- Commands stop after timeout_seconds: 600 by default, at most 3600. Use it for tests, builds and scripts; run dev servers in a shell with pistachio run. A cancelled request stops its command.
- Grants an agent asks for cover only the folder it runs in (and that repository’s worktrees), last for the time it asked for (which you see and approve), end when the agent quits, and can’t include production environments or a whole project. Grant those yourself with pistachio grant.
- Approval panels for requests through the MCP server say they come from an agent.
- Several requests in a row from the same agent in the same folder share one panel while it’s up, and one touch answers them; a grant until the agent quits stops the asking for the rest of the session.
- Reading values, changing or deleting items, earlier values, remote locations and pushes aren’t offered.
A pistachio_run result
```
{
  "content": [{ "type": "text", "text": "exit code 0
--- stdout ---
12 passing" }],
  "structuredContent": {
    "exitCode": 0, "timedOut": false,
    "stdout": "12 passing", "stdoutTruncated": false,
    "stderr": "", "stderrTruncated": false
  },
  "isError": false
}
```
A refusal is a tool error (isError: true) whose structuredContent has error (refused, missing, unreachable, usage), the ids, and for a refusal the grantCommand for the person to run.
## Other MCP servers
An MCP server that your agent starts as a command can get its keys through Pistachio: wrap the command, and keep references in its environment.
.mcp.json
```
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "some-server": {
      "command": "pistachio",
      "args": ["run", "--no-masking", "--", "npx", "-y", "some-mcp-server"],
      "env": { "SOME_API_KEY": "pistachio://SOME_API_KEY" }
    }
  }
}
```
- Use --no-masking: MCP speaks over standard output, which must pass through untouched.
- The server’s process chain includes the agent, so make its items agent-safe or grant them, or each start asks.
- Servers reached over HTTP with a header can’t be wrapped this way.
Agents need the absolute path when ~/.local/bin isn’t on their PATH: use "command": "/Users/you/.local/bin/pistachio".
## Key files
Terminal
```
pistachio run --file ASC_KEY_PATH=shop/production/ASC_P8 -- fastlane beta
```
The command gets the path of a temporary file only you can read, deleted when it exits. In an env file, ASC_KEY_PATH=pistachio-file://shop/production/ASC_P8 does the same.
## What Pistachio can’t do for you
A value you release to a command is in that command’s memory and environment. A command run by an agent can write it to a file, send it over the network, or encode it so masking doesn’t catch it. Masking only hides exact copies, 6 characters or longer, in what the command prints. Agent-safe and grants decide what reaches the command; they can’t control what the command does with it.

---

Page: pistachio:// references and the broker API · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/developers/api.html

# References and API
The formats Pistachio reads and writes: references in your files, the protocol between the command-line tool and the app, and the files it keeps on disk.
Use the command-line tool. pistachio is the supported interface, from any language. The socket protocol below is how it talks to the app; it changes only by adding optional fields, but scripts that speak it directly also take on its approval rules.
## References
FormWhereBecomes
pistachio://IDValues in env files and in the environment of pistachio runThe item’s value
pistachio-file://IDValues in env files and in the environment of pistachio runThe path of a temporary file holding the value, mode 0600, deleted when the command exits
A pistachio:// reference can sit inside a longer value, as in postgres://app:pistachio://shop/production/DB_PASSWORD@db/shop; each one is replaced. A pistachio-file:// reference must be the whole value. ID is NAME or project/environment/NAME, each part letters, digits, _, - and ., at most 64 bytes.
.env.local
```
DATABASE_URL=pistachio://shop/development/DATABASE_URL
SENTRY_DSN=pistachio://SENTRY_DSN
ASC_KEY_PATH=pistachio-file://shop/production/ASC_P8
```
## The broker protocol
The app listens on a Unix socket at ~/Library/Application Support/Latchkey/broker.sock, mode 0600 in a 0700 folder. A client connects, writes one JSON object followed by a newline, and reads one JSON object followed by a newline. Keys are sorted; dates are ISO 8601. Requests say nothing about their caller. The broker asks the kernel instead: the caller’s working folder, command line and parent processes, and, by code signature, whether it’s Pistachio’s own command-line tool. The approval panel and the log show those, and grants are matched against the real folder. A signed pistachio also checks that the socket belongs to the Pistachio app before it sends anything.
Requests are handled one at a time. A request that needs approval waits until you answer, so allow for that in timeouts.
Request
```
{"op":"status"}
```
Response
```
{"info":{"approval":"Touch ID, password","caller":"Pistachio's command-line tool (signature checked)","grants":"0","items":"17","socket":"/Users/you/Library/Application Support/Latchkey/broker.sock","storage":"iCloud Keychain storage (sync status not verified)"},"ok":true}
```
### Operations
opFieldsReturns
statusinfo
listsecrets: item metadata, never values
checknames, intended (the command to test command-limited grants against)agentSafe, granted (with the covering grants), needsApproval, missing. Never asks, never values
getnamesvalues, masked (names to hide in output), denied, missing
setnames (one), value, kind, agentSafe, note, serviceok
updatenames, kind, agentSafe, note, serviceok
rmnamesok, or missing
movenames, project ("" for shared), environmentmoved: old ID to new ID
importitems, replace, sourceadded, replaced, skipped
historynames (one)versions, never values
deletedversions of deleted items
versionversion: a version ID from historyvalues, after approval (always asks)
restoreversionok
forgetnamesok
grantsgrants
grantnames, folder (default: where the caller runs), duration (seconds), session, commands (lists of words), usesgrants
revokenames: a grant ID, or ["all"]info.revoked, or missing
linksnames: optional scopelinks
linknames: the scope, targetlinks
unlinknames: the link IDok
remote-statusnames: the scoperemoteStatus
pushnames: the scope, link, onlypushResults
origin: "mcp" marks a request from pistachio mcp: the approval panel says an agent asked, and a grant it asks for must be its own folder, for the agent’s session, and nothing in production or a whole project. The label is the request’s own claim: it adds limits, never permissions. Unknown op values are refused.
### Responses
Every response has ok. When it’s false, error says why: bad input, a change you didn’t approve, a keychain failure. Reads report per item instead: get answers ok: true with denied for items you refused and missing for IDs that don’t exist, and if anything was denied, no values are released at all. The command-line tool maps these to exit codes 77 and 66.
A refused get
```
{"denied":["shop/production/STRIPE_KEY"],"masked":[],"ok":true,"values":{}}
```
### The item shape
What list returns in secrets, and what pistachio list --json prints:
pistachio list --json
```
[
  {
    "agentSafe" : false,
    "kind" : "password",
    "name" : "shop/development/DATABASE_URL",
    "note" : "",
    "service" : "Neon",
    "updatedAt" : "2026-11-10T21:52:37Z",
    "usedIn" : [
      "/Users/you/Projects/shop/.env.local"
    ]
  }
]
```
FieldMeaning
nameThe item ID
kindtoken, password, key or value
agentSafeRead without asking
noteFree text
serviceWho issued it, optional
usedInFiles that reference it, recorded on import and move, optional
updatedAtWhen the value or settings last changed
### The grant shape
Grant
```
{
  "created": "2026-11-10T20:00:00Z",
  "createdBy": "zsh › claude",
  "expires": "2026-11-10T22:00:00Z",
  "folder": "/Users/you/Projects/shop",
  "id": "k3v9q2",
  "names": ["shop/development/*"],
  "repo": "/Users/you/Projects/shop/.git"
}
```
repo is the repository’s common .git folder, present when the folder is in one; commands run from any of its worktrees are covered.
## The access log
~/Library/Application Support/Latchkey/access.jsonl, mode 0600: one JSON object per line for every read, change and refusal. Never values.
access.jsonl
```
{"chain":["zsh","claude","Terminal"],"command":"pistachio run -- npm test","cwd":"/Users/you/Projects/shop","decision":"allowed (grant k3v9q2)","names":["shop/development/DATABASE_URL"],"op":"get","time":"2026-11-10T20:14:03Z"}
```
FieldMeaning
timeWhen
opThe operation
namesItem IDs involved
decisionWhat happened: allowed and why, denied, refused
chainThe calling process and its parents, nearest first
cwdThe folder the caller ran in, from the kernel
commandThe caller’s command line, from the kernel
programThe calling program’s path, when it isn’t Pistachio’s signed command-line tool
prev, macThe keyed hash (HMAC-SHA256) of the entry before and of this one. pistachio log --verify checks the chain against a key and head only Pistachio can read
## Files and storage
WhereWhat
iCloud Keychain, access group TEAM.io.snackstud.latchkeyItems, earlier values and remote links, as generic passwords in the app’s keychain services. Synced to your Macs.
~/Library/Application Support/Latchkey/broker.sockThe broker socket
~/Library/Application Support/Latchkey/access.jsonlThe access log
The app’s local keychain grant serviceGrants in effect, on this Mac only, changeable only by Pistachio
/Applications/Latchkey.app/Contents/Helpers/latchkeyThe command-line tool, linked from ~/.local/bin/pistachio

---

Page: CLI reference for pistachio and pst · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/developers/cli.html

# CLI reference
Every pistachio command and option. pistachio help prints a summary. Nothing here prints a value except pistachio get.
## Conventions
- pst is the same tool: pst run -- npm test.
- IDs are NAME or project/environment/NAME. Where a command takes several, separate them with commas.
- PATTERN means project/* or project/environment/*.
- Each command that changes items asks for approval once, for everything it touches.
- If the app isn’t running, pistachio starts it hidden and waits. PISTACHIO_NO_LAUNCH=1 fails with 69 instead.
## Running commands
### pistachio run
Synopsis
```
pistachio run [options] -- COMMAND [ARGS...]
```
Starts COMMAND with every pistachio://ID in its environment replaced by the item’s value.
OptionMeaning
--env-file FILELoad KEY=VALUE lines from FILE first. Repeatable.
--env PROJECT/ENVSet the environment’s variables from its record (see Environments). Without a record, or before env migrate has run, it also loads what the older lookup finds: each item in the environment as its name, plus the shared items in the same checkout as its files (as recorded on import), and says so. Repeatable.
--file NAME=IDSet NAME to the path of a temporary file holding the value, readable only by you and deleted when COMMAND exits. NAME=pistachio-file://ID in an env file does the same.
--no-maskingDon’t hide values in COMMAND’s output, and start it directly.
--proxyKeep OPENAI_API_KEY and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY out of COMMAND entirely (see below).
--proxy-models A,BWith --proxy: refuse requests that don’t name one of these models in their JSON body.
--proxy-requests NWith --proxy: refuse requests after N have been forwarded.
--aws-session, --aws-role ARN, --aws-for TIMEGive COMMAND short-lived AWS credentials instead of the long-lived key (see below).
Items that aren’t agent-safe or covered by a grant ask for approval first. Values of secret kinds that are 6 characters or longer are replaced with <concealed by pistachio> in COMMAND’s output, including values split across two chunks; multi-line values are hidden line by line. COMMAND’s exit status becomes pistachio run’s. If COMMAND is killed by a signal, the status is 128 plus the signal.
Examples
```
pistachio run --env-file .env.local -- npm run dev
pistachio run --env shop/development --env shop/vercel.preview -- npm test
pistachio run --file ASC_KEY_PATH=shop/production/ASC_P8 -- fastlane beta
```
Other credentials are delivered normally and are not protected by the proxy. Temporary files are distinct per full item ID.
### pistachio check
Synopsis
```
pistachio check [--env-file FILE]... [--env PROJECT/ENV]... [--file NAME=ID]... [IDS] [--json]
```
What pistachio run with the same options would get without asking (agent-safe or covered by a grant), what would ask you, and what’s missing. Asks nothing and releases nothing. Exits 66 if an item is missing, otherwise 0.
Example
```
$ pistachio check --env-file .env.local
agent-safe        shop/development/PGHOST
granted           shop/development/DATABASE_URL  (grant k3v9q2, 1 hour, 12 minutes left)
asks              shop/development/STRIPE_KEY
```
### pistachio mcp
Serves Pistachio’s tools to an agent over MCP, on standard input and output. See Pistachio’s MCP server.
### Keys that never reach the command: --proxy
With --proxy, a variable that is exactly a reference to an OpenAI or Anthropic key gets a placeholder instead, and OPENAI_BASE_URL or ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL points at a port on this Mac that pistachio run listens on. Requests there that carry the placeholder go to api.openai.com or api.anthropic.com with the real key in its place; anything else is refused. The command can use the key but can’t read, print or send it anywhere else.
Terminal
```
pistachio run --proxy --env shop/development -- npm test
```
It works with programs that use the OpenAI or Anthropic SDKs (or read those base URL variables). The run is refused if a supported key is not a whole reference, its base URL is already set, or the key would also be delivered through another variable or key file; unset custom base URLs first. At least one supported key reference is required.
Only COMMAND and the processes it starts can use the proxy: a request from any other program, even one that knows the placeholder, gets a 403, and the proxy stops when COMMAND exits. A process that detaches from COMMAND (so launchd adopts it) is refused too.
--proxy-models and --proxy-requests narrow what COMMAND may do with the key. With --proxy-models, only requests with a JSON body naming a listed model are forwarded, so GET /v1/models, multipart uploads and compressed bodies are refused. When either is set, pistachio run prints pistachio: proxy limits enforced: ... on standard error. Both need --proxy. For the MCP tool, see Agents and MCP.
Terminal
```
pistachio run --proxy --proxy-models gpt-4o-mini,gpt-4o --proxy-requests 200 --env shop/development -- npm test
```
### Short-lived AWS credentials
With --aws-session, pistachio run signs a request to AWS STS with your long-lived access key (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, both references) and gives COMMAND the temporary credentials STS returns, including AWS_SESSION_TOKEN. --aws-role ARN assumes that role instead. They last 15 minutes unless --aws-for says otherwise (at most 12 hours). The long-lived key never reaches COMMAND, and no AWS CLI is needed. MFA isn’t supported yet.
Terminal
```
pistachio run --aws-role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/dev --aws-for 1h --env shop/development -- terraform plan
```
### pistachio get
Synopsis
```
pistachio get ID
```
Prints one value. Asks unless the item is agent-safe or covered by a grant. Keep agents away from it.
## Items
CommandWhat it does
pistachio list [--project P] [--json]IDs grouped by project and environment, with kind, service, whether agents may read them, and the note. --json prints the same as JSON (see the item shape). Never values.
pistachio set ID [--kind KIND] [--agent-safe] [--note TEXT] [--service NAME]Add or change an item. The value comes from standard input, or a hidden prompt in a terminal. Kinds: token, password, key, value. Replacing a value keeps the old one as a version. Asks.
pistachio update IDS|PATTERN... [--agent-safe yes|no] [--kind KIND] [--service NAME] [--note TEXT] [--fill-sites HOSTS]Change settings on many items with one approval. Values are untouched. --service "" clears the service. --fill-sites vercel.com,app.netlify.com sets the only sites Pistachio for Safari may fill the items on (each covers its subdomains; up to 20); --fill-sites "" goes back to the default: the service’s own site and the deployment platforms.
pistachio rm IDS|PATTERN...Delete items with one approval; they go to Recently Deleted for 30 days. If any named item doesn’t exist, nothing is deleted.
pistachio mv IDS | --from-file FILE --to PROJECT/ENV | --shared [--file FILE]...Move items into a project’s environment, or back to shared, with one approval. Values, settings and history move with them. References are then updated in the files the items came from, each --file, and the --from-file file, which moves every shared item it refers to. If any target ID already exists, nothing moves.
pistachio duplicates [--json]Lists groups of items holding the same value, counted by kind at the top, and what to do about each, with the command to run. See below.
pistachio combine IDS --into NAME|ID [--file FILE]...Makes items holding one value into one shared item, with one approval. See below.
pistachio scan [DIR] [--json], scan --staged, scan --install-hook [--force]Finds env files that still hold plain values. See Scanning env files.
Examples
```
printf %s "$TOKEN" | pistachio set shop/production/STRIPE_KEY --kind token --service Stripe
pistachio update 'shop/development/*' --agent-safe no
pistachio list --project shop --json
```
### pistachio duplicates
Synopsis
```
pistachio duplicates [--json]
```
Lists groups of items holding the same value, counted by kind at the top, and what to do about each, with the command to run:
- production shares a value with another environment: give production its own key;
- several names for one value in one environment (PGHOST and POSTGRES_HOST): keep one item there;
- a shared item already holds it: point the rest at it;
- the same key across projects: combine into one shared item. A suggested name that another group also suggests, or that a shared item already has, gets the first project as a prefix (MANAGER_DATABASE_URL);
- identifiers rather than secrets (IDs, hosts, public keys, web addresses without credentials): mark them plain values.
Values are compared inside Pistachio and never shown; plain values and values shorter than 8 characters are left out. It asks for approval every time (grants and agent-safe settings don’t stand in), and agents can’t ask. --json gives items, advice, summary and into for each group.
### pistachio combine
Synopsis
```
pistachio combine IDS --into NAME|ID [--file FILE]...
```
Makes items holding one value into one shared item NAME, or into one item ID of the environment they’re all in, with one approval. NAME is created from them (agent-safe only if every one was; the service if they agree; where they were used, combined), or must already hold the same value. The others go to Recently Deleted, environment records point at NAME, and references are updated in the files the items were imported from and in each --file. If the values differ, nothing changes. Agents can’t combine.
Example
```
pistachio duplicates
pistachio combine shop/development/OPENAI_API_KEY,blog/development/OPENAI_API_KEY --into OPENAI_API_KEY
```
### pistachio scan
Synopsis
```
pistachio scan [DIR] [--json]
pistachio scan --staged
pistachio scan --install-hook [--force]
```
Finds env files under DIR (default: the current folder; .env, .env.* and *.env, not examples, templates or backups, not in node_modules, build or .git folders) that still hold plain values, and prints each as FILE:LINE NAME with the reason, never a value:
- the value equals a stored item: the line names the item(s). The values are compared inside Pistachio, which receives the values found in the files and returns only item IDs. Like duplicates, it asks every time (grants and agent-safe settings don’t stand in), and agents can’t ask. Plain items and values shorter than 8 characters are left out;
- the value looks secret: a private key, a password or a connection string with credentials, a token with a known prefix (sk_live_, ghp_, AKIA…), or a long value under a name such as *_TOKEN, *_SECRET or *_API_KEY. Identifiers (IDs, hosts, public addresses) and pistachio:// references are not findings. This check is local.
It exits 1 when anything is found, so it works in scripts. If Pistachio can’t compare (not approved, not running), the values that look secret are still reported, and it exits 1. --json gives place, key, reason (stored or looks-secret) and items for each finding.
--staged scans only the lines a commit would add, from the Git index, in env files that are staged.
--install-hook writes a Git pre-commit hook (honoring core.hooksPath, and worktrees) that runs pistachio scan --staged and refuses the commit on findings. A hook that isn’t Pistachio’s is left alone unless --force. If neither pst nor pistachio is on the PATH, the hook says so and lets the commit through. Skip it for one commit with git commit --no-verify.
Examples
```
pistachio scan ~/Projects/shop
pistachio scan --install-hook
```
## Environments
Each environment has a record: its variables, each pointing at an item (shared items too) or holding a plain setting such as PORT=3000. Records sync with your items, so an environment works the same on every Mac, wherever its checkout is. Import, set and mv keep them current.
CommandWhat it does
pistachio env [list], pistachio env show PROJECT/ENV [--json]Records, and one record’s variables. Unconfirmed variables are marked.
pistachio env migrate [--dry-run]Makes or completes records from your items and, where they’re on this Mac, the files they came from. Only adds: a stored variable is never changed, and running it again is safe. Reports conflicts, missing items, missing files and plain values that may be secret. What it found through files is unconfirmed until env confirm. Only numbers up to six digits and true/false are recorded from files without asking you. Asks once.
pistachio env set PROJECT/ENV NAME=pistachio://ID|NAME=VALUE..., env unset, env confirmChange one record. NAME=pistachio://ID points a variable at an item (it must exist); NAME=VALUE is a plain setting. A plain setting that looks secret is refused: save it as an item and point the variable at it. env confirm with no names confirms everything unconfirmed. Asks once.
pistachio env rm PROJECT/ENVForgets an environment’s record, with one approval. Its items stay, and run --env goes back to finding them by ID until a record is made again.
pistachio project [DIR], project link [NAME] [DIR] [--remote R], project unlink NAME [DIR], project listWhich project a checkout is, from its Git remotes (never with credentials). project shows the matching project, its environments, and the export command to run. link remembers the checkout’s origin (or --remote R, or its only remote) as project NAME, by default the folder’s name, so clones on your other Macs are recognized; it asks. A remote belongs to one project; unlinking a project’s last remote forgets the project. A match only names the project: it never releases a value or widens a grant. A match through a remote other than origin, as a fork has, is flagged and never taken as the project.
## Export
### pistachio export
Synopsis
```
pistachio export PROJECT/ENV [--out FILE [--merge [--yes] | --replace]] [--values [--clipboard]]
```
Writes the environment’s env file from its record: pistachio:// references and plain settings, sorted by name, to standard output or FILE.
- An existing FILE is left alone, and the variables that would change are named, unless --merge or --replace. A symbolic link or anything but a regular file is refused. The file is written beside its destination and renamed into place, so it’s never half-written.
- --merge updates the variables the record has, appends the ones missing, and leaves every other byte of the file as it is: comments, blank lines, order, variables Pistachio doesn’t manage, line endings, a last line without one. A variable already holding the value is left as written; an updated line keeps its indentation and export and loses an inline comment. It lists the names it will add and update, then asks to go ahead (--yes skips that; without a terminal --yes is required). The file must be UTF-8 KEY=VALUE lines, and it’s refused if it changes while waiting. Nothing to change writes nothing. A file that doesn’t exist yet is created, as without --merge. With --values, a variable already in the file is listed as an update before its value is known, and a merged file becomes readable only by you.
- --replace rewrites the whole file, losing its comments and other variables.
- --values writes the values themselves, in plain text. It needs --out (or --clipboard), asks every time with the file named (no grant, agent-safe setting or earlier approval stands in), writes the file readable only by you, and the access log records which items went to which file, never the values. Agents can’t use it. Inside a Git checkout the file must be ignored and not tracked, or nothing is asked or written; a file in a folder that syncs to iCloud Drive, Dropbox, Google Drive or OneDrive gets a warning, since the values would leave the Mac.
- --values --clipboard copies the environment as an env block (no header comment) for a dashboard that takes a pasted one, instead of writing a file. It asks every time, naming the environment and that the values go to the clipboard. The copy is for this Mac only (not Universal Clipboard), marked concealed and transient so clipboard managers skip it, and cleared after 60 seconds if nothing else was copied meanwhile. Agents and Safari can’t copy, nor can a request forwarded over SSH (the clipboard would be on the other computer). The log records “copied to the clipboard”, never the values; unlike a file, a copy can’t be traced afterwards.
- Unconfirmed variables and references to missing items are noted on standard error.
Examples
```
pistachio export shop/development --out .env.local --merge
pistachio export shop/development --values --clipboard
```
## Importing
Synopsis
```
pistachio import FILE... [options]
```
OptionMeaning
--batch LISTAlso import the files listed in LIST, one path per line (# comments allowed).
--scan DIRAlso import every .env and .env.* under DIR, skipping examples, templates, backups, and dependency, build and .git folders.
--project P, --env EPlace items here instead of what the repository and file name imply.
--sharedImport as shared items named after their keys.
--share-identicalWith several files, make a name with the same value in every file one shared item.
--rewriteReplace each imported value in its file with its reference.
--replaceOverwrite items that already exist (old values are kept as versions).
--dry-runShow what would happen, with a count per class and each setting it would leave; send nothing.
--only KEY,...Import only these keys (one file only).
--kind KIND, --kind KEY=KINDKind for all keys, or one.
--class KEY=secret|setting|publicChange how a line is classed (see below). --kind KEY=KIND also decides the class.
--agent-safe KEY,... or allMark keys agent-safe.
--agent-safe-pattern PATTERN,...Import matching names as agent-safe plain values.
--skip PATTERN,...Leave matching names alone.
--no-default-skipImport VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN, VERCEL_* and TURBO_* too.
Imports support quoted multiline values and refuse malformed syntax before saving anything. Rewriting replaces the complete assignment and stops if the file changed while approval was pending.
### Classes
Each line is classed before anything is saved:
ClassExamplesWhat import does
SecretTokens, passwords, connection strings with credentials, key blocksSaved masked
SettingPORT, NODE_ENV, LOG_LEVEL, *_ENABLED, *_PORT, true/false valuesLeft in the file
PublicNEXT_PUBLIC_*, VITE_*, PUBLIC_*, EXPO_PUBLIC_*, REACT_APP_*, publishable and public keys, IDs and hosts, web addresses with no credentialsSaved as a plain value (not masked, not agent-safe unless you say so)
Referencepistachio://...Left alone
A value that carries credentials (a key block, a URL with a user or password) is a secret whatever its name says, and anything unclear is a secret. Settings stay in the file, so --rewrite doesn’t touch them. In the app, the Class column of the import sheet does the same as --class. Classes aren’t remembered between imports yet.
Example
```
pistachio import .env.local --dry-run
pistachio import .env.local --rewrite --class FEATURE_FLAGS=setting
```
## History
CommandWhat it does
pistachio history IDEarlier values: when, why (replaced, deleted, replaced by a restore) and by whom. Never values.
pistachio restore ID [--version N]Put back version N (1 is the most recent), or bring back a deleted item with its settings. The current value is kept as a version first. Asks.
pistachio deletedItems deleted in the last 30 days, with days left.
pistachio forget IDSDelete earlier values for good. Asks.
## Grants
CommandWhat it does
pistachio grant IDS [--folder DIR] [--for TIME] [--session] [--command CMD]... [--once]Let commands run from DIR (default: here), the folders inside it and that repository’s worktrees read these items without asking. TIME is like 30m, 2h, 1d, or always for a grant that lasts until revoked; default 1 hour, no maximum. IDS can include patterns. Asks once.
pistachio grantsGrants in effect, with time left and any limits.
pistachio revoke ID or allEnd a grant, or all of them. Doesn’t ask.
Narrow a grant with --session (it ends when the agent you run it under quits, and covers only programs started under it), --command "npm test" (only pistachio run of that command, read from the signed tool’s own command line), or --once (one request). The approval panel offers the same: until claude quits and Only for ….
## Rotating
CommandWhat it does
pistachio touched [--since 24h] [--by NAME] [--grant ID] [--json]Items Pistachio released in that time: to anything, to programs under NAME (such as claude), or under one grant. From the access log; never values.
pistachio rotate IDS|PATTERN... | --touched [...] [--open] [--push]Replace items one by one: ends grants that cover them, shows where to make each new key (--open opens it), asks for the new value (the old one stays in history), then pushes to linked environments with --push.
After an agent session
```
pistachio touched --since 4h --by claude
pistachio rotate --touched --since 4h --by claude --open --push
```
Pistachio can’t make the new key for you: Stripe, GitHub, OpenAI and most services issue keys only in their dashboards. It takes you to the page, saves what you paste, and puts it everywhere it’s linked.
## Remote locations
CommandWhat it does
pistachio remote list [PROJECT/ENV]Links, with when each was last pushed.
pistachio remote link PROJECT/ENV SERVICE KEY=VALUE...Link an environment. SERVICE is vercel, github, railway, fly or ssh (host= and script=; see a service on a Linux server). Asks.
pistachio remote unlink LINKRemove a link. Doesn’t ask.
pistachio remote status PROJECT/ENVNames missing on each side, and values changed since the last push.
pistachio push PROJECT/ENV [--to LINK] [--only IDS] [--dry-run]Push values with each service’s own tool, values on standard input. Asks every time; production needs its own confirmation in the app. Nothing is deployed.
ServiceKeysTool
vercelenvironment= (development, preview or production), and project= or dir=; optional branch= for one preview branchvercel
githubrepo=owner/repo; optional environment= (leave out for repository secrets)gh
railwayenvironment=, service=, and project= or dir=railway
flyapp=flyctl
## The log
CommandWhat it does
pistachio log [--limit 20]Recent access log entries: time, what, decision, items, who, folder and command. Never values; likely secrets in command lines are redacted.
pistachio log --verifyChecks the log’s chain: exits 0 if every entry is as Pistachio wrote it, 1 with the first line that isn’t.
## Status
Synopsis
```
pistachio status
```
Where values are kept, how you approve, how many items and grants, and the socket path.
## Environment variables
VariableMeaning
PISTACHIO_NO_LAUNCH=1Don’t start the app if it isn’t running; fail with exit 69 instead.
PISTACHIO_SOCKET=PATHConnect to a socket forwarded over SSH from the Mac running Pistachio (see from another Mac).
## Exit codes
CodeMeaning
0Done
64Wrong usage
66No item with that ID
69The Pistachio app can’t be reached
73A file couldn’t be rewritten
77Refused: not agent-safe, not approved, no grant
127The command couldn’t start
On 66 and 77, Pistachio prints the item IDs and what to do, including the pistachio grant command that would allow the refused items.

Page: Developer docs: how Pistachio fits together · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/developers/

# Pistachio for developers
Everything you can script: the pistachio command-line tool, the references your files hold, the protocol the tool speaks to the app, and how to put agents and MCP servers behind it.
## The pieces
- The app holds the keychain. It runs the broker, shows approval panels, and keeps the log, grants and history. Only the signed app can read Pistachio’s keychain access group.
- pistachio, the command-line tool, asks the app for everything over a Unix socket. It starts the app in the background if it isn’t running.
- References such as pistachio://shop/production/DATABASE_URL go in env files and environment variables in place of values.
How it fits together
```
pistachio (CLI)
   │  JSON over a Unix socket
   ▼
Broker (in the app) ──► iCloud Keychain
   ├─ approval panel, then Touch ID
   ├─ grants: keychain, this Mac only
   ├─ access log: access.jsonl (never values)
   └─ remote pushes: vercel, gh, railway, flyctl,
      or the services' APIs with a token item
```
## Where to start
Quickstart
Install the tool, import an env file, run a command, grant a folder.
CLI reference
Every command and option, environment variables and exit codes.
Agents and MCP
Instructions for coding agents, narrower grants, keys an agent can use without reading, rotation after a session, SSH, and Pistachio’s MCP server.
References and API
The reference formats, the broker protocol, the access log, and the files Pistachio keeps.
## Item IDs
An item is either shared, NAME, or belongs to one environment of a project, project/environment/NAME. Each part is letters, digits, _, - and ., at most 64 bytes. For an item, the ID is the only place its project and environment are stored.
Environments can be any name; development, preview, staging, production and test sort first. Use names like vercel.preview to tell apart the same environment in different places.
KindForMasked in output
tokenAPI tokens and keys, one lineYes
passwordPasswords and connection strings, one lineYes
keyKey material: SSH, GPG, .p8, .pem. Multi-lineYes, line by line
valueNot secret: host names, account IDsNo
## What’s released without asking
A read is released without a prompt only when the item is agent-safe (No Approval in the app), or a grant covers the folder, session and command as applicable. Allow Once authorizes one request; approvals are not cached. Revoking a grant stops future reads through it, but cannot recall released values. Everything else shows the approval panel, then Touch ID, Apple Watch or your password. Earlier values always ask. Changes (set, update, delete, move, import, restore, push) always ask, once per request: the Touch ID sheet alone, with the panel behind its Details… button (pushes show the panel first).

Page: Quickstart: install, import and run · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/developers/quickstart.html

# Quickstart
From an env file full of secrets to a command that gets them at start-up, in four steps.
## 1. Install
Download the latest disk image and drag Pistachio to Applications, or install it with Homebrew: brew tap zachshallbetter/latchkey, brew trust zachshallbetter/latchkey, then brew install --cask latchkey. The cask adds both commands for you. With the disk image, open it and choose Pistachio › Install Command Line Tool…, which links ~/.local/bin/pistachio, and pst for short, to the copy inside the app so it updates with the app. Make sure ~/.local/bin is on your PATH; in zsh, echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc does it. With the Mac App Store version, see the command-line tool.
Terminal
```
pistachio status
```
You should see storage: iCloud Keychain storage (sync status not verified).
## 2. Import an env file
Look first. A dry run prints names and where each would go, never values:
Terminal
```
cd ~/Projects/shop
pistachio import .env.local --dry-run
```
The dry run also classes each line: secret, setting (such as PORT, left in the file), public value (such as NEXT_PUBLIC_*, saved as a plain value) or existing reference. It counts each class and lists each setting it would leave. Change a line with --class KEY=secret|setting|public.
Then import, and replace each value in the file with its reference. The project is named after the repository; the environment comes from the file name (.env.local is development).
Terminal
```
pistachio import .env.local --rewrite
```
.env.local
```
DATABASE_URL=pistachio://shop/development/DATABASE_URL
STRIPE_KEY=pistachio://shop/development/STRIPE_KEY
```
Imports support quoted multiline values and refuse malformed syntax before saving anything. Rewriting replaces the complete assignment and stops if the file changed while approval was pending.
The dry run, then the import: one approval, and each value in the file becomes its reference. Here --skip PORT leaves a plain setting as it is. Example data; the output is what Pistachio prints.
Every project at once: pistachio import --scan ~/Projects --dry-run, then again without --dry-run. Or pistachio import --batch files.txt, one path per line. Either way, one approval. See the import options.
## 3. Run a command
Terminal
```
pistachio run --env-file .env.local -- npm run dev
pistachio run --env shop/development -- npm test      # no env file needed
```
pst run reads the references, asks Pistachio for the values, and starts the command with them in its environment; anything it prints of them is concealed. Example data; the output is what Pistachio prints.
Reads ask unless a grant or the No Approval setting permits them. Values that reach the command’s output are replaced with <concealed by pistachio>. The command’s exit status becomes pistachio run’s.
## 4. Let an agent work
Before you step away, allow the folder for a while. Commands run from it, its subfolders and the repository’s worktrees read these items without asking until the grant ends.
Terminal
```
pistachio grant 'shop/development/*' --folder ~/Projects/shop --for 2h
pistachio grants
pistachio revoke all
```
Then tell the agent how to run things; see instructions for agents.

Page: Features: env references, Keychain and agent access · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/features.html

# Credentials kept by name in Keychain, and filled in when a command starts.
Credentials that have IDs, history and a home outside any one project. Env files that hold references. Environments that rebuild on another Mac. Commands and agents that use values only when you've said so, and a record of every time they did.
- Credentials
- Environments
- Devices
- Agents and tools
- Integrations
- Visibility
- Pro
In this build Works in the development preview.Pending Built but not yet verified for release, or not built yet.Everything on this page is free. What Pro addsScenes replay what Pistachio prints and shows, with example data.
Credentials
## Every credential has a name, a place and a past.
An item is project/environment/NAME, or just NAME when it's shared by every project. Its kind, service and note travel with it, and replacing its value keeps the old one.
The Pistachio window, with example data. With scripts on, it works: search, filter by type or environment, pick a project or service in the sidebar, and open an item. It lists:
- shop: DATABASE_URL, STRIPE_KEY, PGHOST and NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL for development; DATABASE_URL for preview, not pushed yet; DATABASE_URL and STRIPE_KEY for production, the key changed since its last push
- blog: ADMIN_PASSWORD, SENTRY_DSN and GITHUB_TOKEN
- api: the ASC_P8 key file and API_BASE_URL
- Shared: OPENAI_API_KEY and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
Opening an item shows its value (hidden until Touch ID), reference, type, access, service, project, environment, note, location, history and recent activity. Review lists what may need a look.
The Pistachio window, working with example data: search, filter by type or environment, pick a project or service, and open an item to see its reference, access, location, history and recent activity. Revealing or copying a value asks for Touch ID. The values are made up.
### Store and organize In this build
Tokens, passwords, key files and plain values, grouped by project and environment in the app and the CLI. The value is read from standard input or a hidden prompt.
```
pst set shop/development/STRIPE_KEY --kind token --service Stripe
```
Items
### Share one value across projects In this build
Importing many projects at once, a key with the same value everywhere becomes one shared item that every file refers to. Rotating it is then one change.
```
pst import --scan ~/Projects --share-identical --dry-run
```
Importing
### Move between environments In this build
Values, settings and history move together, and the references in the files they came from are updated.
```
pst mv OPENAI_API_KEY --to shop/development
```
Moving items
### History and restore In this build
The last 10 values of each item, and deleted items for 30 days. History lists when and why, never values; Forget History deletes old values for good.
```
pst history shop/development/STRIPE_KEY
pst restore shop/development/STRIPE_KEY --version 1
```
History
### Find duplicates and combine them In this build
One approval compares values inside Pistachio and says what to do: give production its own key, or combine the rest into one shared item. Files follow, and the originals go to Recently Deleted.
```
pst duplicates
pst combine shop/development/STRIPE_KEY blog/development/STRIPE_KEY --into STRIPE_KEY
```
Duplicates
### Catch plain values before a commit In this build
pst scan finds env files that still hold a stored value or something that looks secret, and prints file, line and item, never the value. The pre-commit hook refuses those commits.
```
pst scan ~/Projects
pst scan --install-hook
```
Scanning
Environments
## References in your files. Values in Keychain.
Each environment has a record of its variables: each points at an item or holds a plain setting like PORT=3000. Records sync with your items, so a checkout anywhere can get its env file back.
### Import, then rewrite
The dry run shows where each value goes and sends nothing. One approval saves them, and --rewrite puts a pistachio:// reference where each value was. Comments, order and file permissions are kept.
### Import one file or every project In this build
The project comes from the repository's folder, the environment from the file name. Each line is classed as a secret, a setting, a public value or an existing reference: settings like PORT stay in the file, public values are saved plain, and anything unclear is a secret.
```
pst import --scan ~/Projects --agent-safe-pattern 'NEXT_PUBLIC_*' --dry-run
```
Importing
### Run without a file In this build
--env loads the environment's record, which suits a fresh worktree with no .env. Key files arrive as a temporary path only you can read.
```
pst run --env shop/development -- npm test
pst run --file ASC_KEY_PATH=shop/production/ASC_P8 -- fastlane beta
```
Running commands
### Export an env file In this build
Writes the environment's file from its record, or --merges into the one you have, keeping comments, order and other variables. --values --clipboard copies an env block for a dashboard; it asks every time and clears after 60 seconds.
```
pst export shop/development --out .env.local --merge
```
Export
### Recognize a checkout In this build
A project is linked to its Git remotes, so a clone under any folder name knows which project it is. A match only names the project; it never releases a value or widens a grant.
```
pst project link shop
pst project
```
Projects
Devices
## The environment travels with the project. The credential stays in your vault.
Values, versions, environment records and project links are keychain items in Pistachio's own access group. iCloud Keychain carries them, end to end encrypted, to every Mac signed in to your Apple Account that has Pistachio installed.
### Clone, export, run
On the next Mac the environment record is already there: pst project recognizes the clone and pst export writes its env file. Grants stay on the Mac where you made them.
Second-Mac test pending
### Signed app access In this build
Only the signed Pistachio app can read its keychain group. The pst tool never touches the keychain; it checks the app's signature before sending anything.
Storage and sync
### Use it from another Mac over SSH In this build
Forward the app's socket. Each read without the No Approval setting asks you on your own Mac; local grants don't apply over the connection. Direct download only, for now.
```
export PISTACHIO_SOCKET=/tmp/pistachio-$USER.sock
```
From another Mac over SSH
### Locks like Passwords In this build
The window locks when Pistachio opens, after 5 minutes in the background and when the Mac sleeps; Touch ID unlocks it. Approvals for commands and agents still work while it's locked.
App lock
### Intel Macs Pending
The app is built for Apple silicon and Intel. The release hasn't been tried on an Intel Mac yet.
Install
### Updates itself In this build
The direct download checks for updates with Sparkle, or install and upgrade with Homebrew. It sends no system profile; the Mac App Store version updates through the store.
```
brew install --cask latchkey
```
Installing
Agents and tools
## Grant access for the task. Revoke it when the task is done.
Agents run commands through pst run. You decide what reaches those commands: agent-safe items, grants for a folder and a time, or an approval each time.
### Ask, allow, and ask again when it matters
The panel shows the agent, the programs it runs through, the folder and the command, all from macOS, with Touch ID right in it: touch the sensor from whatever app you're in. Several requests from the same agent share one panel and one touch. A folder grant until the agent quits covers its next runs; a production item isn't covered, so it asks.
### Grants with limits In this build
For a folder (and its repository's worktrees), for any length of time, until the agent quits, until you revoke it, for one command, or for one request. Kept where only Pistachio can change them.
```
pst grant 'shop/development/*' --session --for 4h
pst grant 'shop/development/*' --command "npm test" --for 2h
```
Grants
### Check before a slow run In this build
What a run would get without asking, what would ask you, and what's missing. Asks nothing, releases nothing.
```
pst check --env shop/development
```
pst check
### MCP server In this build
Status, list, check, run, project, export references and request a grant, for clients without a shell. There's no secret-read tool; grants it asks for cover only its own folder, end when the agent quits, and never include production.
```
claude mcp add pistachio -- ~/.local/bin/pistachio mcp
```
Pistachio's MCP server
### Skill and plugin Pending
The Pistachio skill tells an agent to run through pst run, never print values, and stop on 77 or 66. It works from a local checkout. The repository is public, so the marketplace install should work, though it hasn't been tried end to end yet.
```
/plugin marketplace add /path/to/pistachio
```
Skills and plugins
### Masked output In this build
A value of a secret kind, 6 characters or longer, that the command prints becomes <concealed by pistachio>, even split across chunks. Transformed values aren't caught.
Where protection ends
Integrations
## From the dashboard where a key is made to the platform that runs it.
Save a new key from the page that shows it, push values to deployment platforms with their own tools, and keep some keys out of the command entirely.
### Capture credentials when they're issued
When a provider shows you a new key, Pistachio for Safari can recognize it and offer to save it: a Save to Pistachio button sits on the box that holds it. You choose what to save, where it goes and its name; approve, and the panel gives you the reference to use. Spotting happens in the page and nothing leaves it until you press Save. Detection depends on page permissions and supported patterns.
What the extension can and can't reach
### Deployment platforms In this build
Link an environment to Vercel, GitHub Actions, Railway or Fly, see names missing on either side, and push with each service's own tool. A service on your own Linux server can take its credentials over ssh, one file each. Every push asks; production needs a second confirmation. Pushes run in the app.
```
pst remote link shop/production fly app=shop-api
pst remote status shop/production
pst push shop/production --dry-run
```
Remote locations
### Fill a field from Pistachio In this build
In a field that takes a key, a badge offers the items that may be filled on that site: the item's service and the deployment platforms, or the sites you choose. Touch ID every time.
```
pst update shop/production/PAYMENTS_KEY --fill-sites vercel.com
```
pst update
### Key proxy In this build
OpenAI and Anthropic keys stay in pst run; the command gets a placeholder and a local base URL, and the real key goes only to the provider's host. It serves only the command and what it started, and can limit models and requests.
```
pst run --proxy --proxy-models gpt-5 --proxy-requests 50 --env shop/development -- npm test
```
--proxy
### Short-lived AWS credentials In this build
STS credentials that expire after 15 minutes by default, while the long-lived key stays in Pistachio. MFA isn't supported yet.
```
pst run --aws-role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/dev -- terraform plan
```
AWS
### Other MCP servers In this build
An MCP server started as a command can get its keys through Pistachio: wrap the command and keep references in its environment.
```
"command": "pistachio",
"args": ["run", "--no-masking", "--", "npx", "-y", "some-mcp-server"]
```
Other MCP servers
Visibility
## Know what read what, and prove the record wasn't edited.
Every read, change, grant, move, import and push is logged with the program chain and folder, never a value. Each entry is chained to the last, so an edit or deletion shows.
### History, the log and its check
pst history lists earlier values by when, why and who. pst log --verify checks the access log's chain and names the first line that isn't as Pistachio wrote it.
### After an agent session In this build
Every key released to programs an agent started, from the access log, then a guided rotation that ends the grants covering them.
```
pst touched --since 4h --by claude
pst rotate --touched --since 4h --by claude --open
```
Rotating
### Activity and the menu bar In this build
Every request in the app's Activity, with what asked and from where; the menu bar panel shows the latest and searches your items. The same log is in the terminal.
```
pst log --limit 20
```
The app
### Expiry and provider-side usage Pending
Pistachio records what it released, not what a service saw. Expiry dates, validity checks and provider-side usage aren't tracked yet; until they are, a note on the item can carry the date.
```
pst update shop/production/STRIPE_KEY --note "expires March 2027"
```
Where protection ends
Pistachio Pro
## Everything above is free. Pro adds four sets of tools.
Pro is planned as a one-time in-app purchase in the Mac App Store, $79 with updates included. None of it is sold before it exists, and none of what's above is planned to move behind it, duplicates, scanning, rotation and pushing to services included.
### Agent controls Planned
Secret requests: an agent asks for a missing key, you paste it in the app, and the agent gets back only the reference. And a hook that stops commands like cat .env and printenv.
### Recovery and migration Planned
Importers for 1Password and Bitwarden through their command-line tools, and for the Passwords app's export, plus an encrypted backup with a matching restore.
### Rotation and lifecycle Planned
Last-used dates from the log, an expiry date per item with reminders, a list of keys nothing has read in 90 days, and leak alerts from GitHub secret scanning.
### Provider integrations Planned
Each key's origin: the service that issued it, the console where it's managed, who made it and when it was last rotated.
Compare free and Pro
## Stop being the credential courier.
Keep your projects, credentials and coding agents working together, with access you can inspect and control. Pistachio is free to download and use, and the core is meant to stay free. Pro will add more for a one-time price in the Mac App Store.

Page: Audit which programs read your secrets · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/guides/audit-secret-access.html

Guide · Audit
# See which programs read your secrets
A secret sitting in a file can be read by anything that can open the file, and nothing records it. When a key leaks, you want to know who read it.
By Zach ShallbetterPublished 14 November 2026Needs the command-line tool
In shortOpen Activity in the app or run pst log to see each read with the program chain, folder and command. Run pst log --verify to check that no entry was changed, removed or added.
## Why plain files can't answer this
A .env file records nothing about who opened it. A leaked key could have come from your editor, a test run, a script, or an agent working in the folder. Without a record you rotate everything and guess.
With Pistachio, values are read through the app, and the app logs each read, change, grant, move, import and push. The log holds the program chain and the folder. It does not hold values.
## Read the record
### Look in Activity
In the app, Activity has search, and filters by event and project, grouped by day. An entry's detail shows the action, the items, the decision, who asked and through which programs, the folder and the command.
### Read the log from the terminal
The same entries are available from the command line. --limit takes 0 through 1000.
Terminal
```
pst log --limit 20
```
pst log prints one readable line per entry. The file behind it, ~/Library/Application Support/Latchkey/access.jsonl, holds one JSON object per line. The fields to read are op (what happened), names (which items), decision (allowed or approved, with why; or denied or refused), chain (the calling program's parent processes, nearest first), cwd and command. This one is an example:
Example entry
```
{"chain":["zsh","claude","Terminal"],"command":"pistachio run -- npm test","cwd":"/Users/you/Projects/shop","decision":"allowed (grant k3v9q2)","names":["shop/development/DATABASE_URL"],"op":"get","time":"2026-11-10T20:14:03Z"}
```
Real entries also carry prev and mac, the hash chain that --verify checks.
### List what one program touched
To ask what was released to programs started under a name, such as an agent, use touched. It reads the access log on this Mac, and counts reads that were allowed or approved.
Terminal
```
pst touched --since 24h --by claude
```
### Check the log wasn't edited
Each entry carries a keyed hash of itself and the entry before it. The key lives in your keychain, where only Pistachio can read it. Verifying checks the whole chain.
Terminal
```
pst log --verify
```
When every entry is as Pistachio wrote it, it prints intact: N signed entries and exits 0. Otherwise it exits 1 and names the first line that isn't, with the reason. It finds an entry that was changed, removed or added, and a log cut short.
### Check an item's earlier values
For one item, history lists earlier values by when, why (changed, deleted or restored) and by whom. It never prints the values. Pistachio keeps the last 10 earlier values of each item.
Terminal
```
pst history shop/development/STRIPE_KEY
```
## What this doesn't do
- The log can't stop a program running as you from deleting the file. It can only show that it happened.
- It records what Pistachio released, not what a service saw. A command that has a value can do what it likes with it.
- The caller chain is informative, not proof. The caller itself is checked by signature, but its parents are named by their files, and file names can be faked. Judge an entry by its folder and command too.
- Command lines in the log have likely secrets replaced with <redacted>. That is a heuristic, not a guarantee, so keep secret values out of command arguments.
More detail is in the log, history and Security.
## Related
Rotate the keys an AI agent touchedList what an agent was given, then replace each key in one pass.Give coding agents API keys without handing them overApprovals, grants, and keys an agent can use but never read.

Page: Give coding agents API keys without handing them over · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/guides/coding-agents-and-api-keys.html

Guide · Coding agents
# Give coding agents API keys without handing them over
An agent that runs your tests needs the keys your tests use. It doesn't need to see them, keep them, or have them pasted into a chat window.
By Zach ShallbetterPublished 14 November 2026Needs the command-line tool
In shortKeep pistachio:// references in your env files and tell the agent to run commands through pistachio run. Each read asks you with Touch ID, showing the agent, folder and command, unless a grant you made covers it. For OpenAI and Anthropic keys, --proxy lets the command call the API without ever holding the key.
## The usual shortcuts
Pasting a key into the conversation puts it in a transcript. Leaving it in .env lets the agent read the file, and so print, log or commit it. Exporting it in your shell hands it to everything that shell starts, for as long as it runs.
## Set it up
### Put references in the env files
Import the files so they hold pistachio:// references rather than values.
### Tell the agent how to run things
Add this to CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md or your agent's instructions:
Agent instructions
```
Secrets are in Pistachio. Env files hold pistachio:// references, not values.
Run anything that needs secrets as
`pistachio run --env-file .env.local -- <command>`.
Never run `pistachio get`, never print the environment, and never read or
write values in .env files. If pistachio exits with 77 (refused) or 66
(missing), stop and ask; don't retry.
```
### Approve when it asks
When the agent runs pistachio run, the approval panel names the agent, the programs it runs through, the folder and the full command. Choose to allow once, allow from that folder for a while, or Deny, then touch the sensor: Touch ID listens right in the panel, from whatever app you're in. Several requests the agent makes in a row share one panel, so one touch answers them all, and each can be denied on its own. A refused run exits with 77 and prints the exact pistachio grant command that would allow it.
### Grant before you step away
Terminal
```
pst grant 'shop/development/*' --session --for 4h
pst grant 'shop/development/*' --command "npm test" --for 2h
```
A session grant ends when the agent quits; a command grant covers only that command. Every read under a grant is listed in Activity, and you can revoke it early.
## Keys the agent can use but never read
Terminal
```
pst run --proxy --env shop/development -- npm test
```
With --proxy, the command gets a placeholder and a local address, and the real OpenAI or Anthropic key is added only to requests bound for that provider. --proxy-models and --proxy-requests limit which models it may name and how many calls it may make.
## After the session
Terminal
```
pst touched --since 4h --by claude
pst rotate --touched --since 4h --by claude --open
```
See every key released to programs the agent started, then replace the ones you'd rather it no longer knew. Rotation ends the grants that covered them.
## What this doesn't do
Approvals and grants decide what reaches a command. They can't control what the command does with a value once it has it. Keep grants narrow and short, and deny requests you don't recognize.
## Related
Hide your OpenAI or Anthropic key from an AI agentLet a command call OpenAI or Anthropic without holding the key.Rotate the keys an AI agent touchedList what an agent was given, then replace each key in one pass.

Page: Find the same API key in many projects · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/guides/duplicate-api-keys.html

Guide · Duplicates
# Find the same API key in many projects
Over time one key gets pasted into several projects, and the production key often ends up in a development file too. Pistachio can tell you where the same value is stored twice.
By Zach ShallbetterPublished 14 November 2026Needs the command-line tool
In shortRun pst duplicates. It compares values inside Pistachio, groups the items that hold the same one, and prints what to do about each group, with the command to run where one applies: give production its own key, or combine the rest with pst combine.
## Why it matters
Copies pile up. You import a second project and reuse the key. When production shares a key with development, every place that holds the development copy holds the production key too, and rotating it means finding every copy.
Pistachio stores each key as an item, so it can compare them. The comparison happens inside the app. You are never shown a value.
## Find and fix them
### Run the check
Terminal
```
pst duplicates
```
It asks for approval every time, and the approval says it is comparing values. Grants and agent-safe settings do not stand in, and agents cannot ask. Plain values and values shorter than 8 characters are left out. The result is counted by kind at the top, then one group per shared value, each with advice and, where one applies, the command to run. The app does the same under Review › Find Duplicates….
### Give production its own key
When production shares a value with another environment, make a new key for production in the service's own dashboard. Pistachio cannot issue it for you. Then save it over the production item. The value is read from standard input or a hidden prompt, and the old one stays as a version.
Terminal
```
pst set shop/production/STRIPE_KEY
```
Development keeps the old key, and production now has one of its own.
### Combine a key used across projects
When the same key sits in several projects, combine the items into one shared item. The IDs here are examples.
Terminal
```
pst combine shop/development/OPENAI_API_KEY,blog/development/OPENAI_API_KEY --into OPENAI_API_KEY
```
One approval does the work. Environment records point at the shared item, references are updated in the files the items were imported from, and the originals go to Recently Deleted for 30 days. If the values differ, nothing changes. The suggested name gets the first project as a prefix, such as MANAGER_DATABASE_URL, when another group suggests the same name or a shared item already has it.
### Tidy the rest
The advice also covers two other cases. Several names for one value in one environment, such as PGHOST and POSTGRES_HOST, should be one item. Identifiers rather than secrets, such as IDs, hosts and public keys, should be marked as plain values. The command for each is printed with the group.
## Check the result
Run pst duplicates again to see what is left. For the projects you have not imported yet, pst import --scan ~/Projects --share-identical --dry-run shows which names hold the same value in every file that has them. It needs at least two files.
## What this doesn't do
- It finds what Pistachio has stored. An env file that has not been imported is not compared; the scan check covers those.
- Combining reduces the copies. It does not make the key any less shared, so rotating it still affects every project that uses it.
- Pistachio cannot create the new production key. Stripe, GitHub, OpenAI and most services only issue keys in their own dashboards.
- combine changes nothing when the values differ, and agents cannot run it.
The duplicates and combine reference has the full option list.
## Related
Keep API keys out of your .env filesMove values into iCloud Keychain and leave references in the file.Block commits that contain secretsRefuse commits that add plain secrets to env files.

Page: How to keep API keys out of .env files on a Mac · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/guides/env-files-without-secrets.html

Guide · Env files
# Keep API keys out of your .env files
An env file that holds real keys gets copied, synced, pasted and read by every tool in the folder. Keep the names in the file and the values in your Mac's iCloud Keychain instead.
By Zach ShallbetterPublished 14 November 2026Needs the command-line tool
In shortRun pst import .env.local --rewrite. Each secret moves into iCloud Keychain and the file keeps a pistachio:// reference in its place. Then start the project with pst run --env-file .env.local -- npm run dev, and Pistachio fills the values in for that command only.
## Where plain values leak
A .env file is ignored by Git, but nothing else ignores it. Backups and cloud-synced folders copy it, screen shares show it, it gets pasted into chat to "just get the build working", and any program you run in the project, a coding agent included, can open it. Rotating a key means finding every copy.
## Move the values into Keychain
### Install Pistachio and its command-line tool
Download it free or install it with Homebrew, whose cask adds pistachio and its short name pst. With the disk image, open it once and choose Pistachio › Install Command Line Tool…. With the Mac App Store version, see the command-line tool.
### Preview the import
Terminal
```
pst import .env.local --dry-run
```
The dry run prints item IDs and counts, never values. Each line is classed first: secrets are saved masked, settings such as PORT stay in the file, public values such as NEXT_PUBLIC_* are saved as plain values, and anything unclear is treated as a secret.
### Import and rewrite the file
Terminal
```
pst import .env.local --rewrite
```
One Touch ID approval saves everything. Comments, order and the settings stay as they were:
.env.local, after
```
STRIPE_KEY=pistachio://shop/development/STRIPE_KEY
DATABASE_URL=pistachio://shop/development/DATABASE_URL
PORT=3000
```
### Run the project the same way as before
Terminal
```
pst run --env-file .env.local -- npm run dev
```
Your app still reads process.env.STRIPE_KEY; the value is filled in when the command starts and never written back to the file.
### Catch the next plain value before it's committed
Terminal
```
pst scan --install-hook
```
The pre-commit hook refuses a commit that adds an env file line holding a stored value or something that looks secret. It names the file, line and item, never the value.
## Many projects at once
Terminal
```
pst import --scan ~/Projects --share-identical --dry-run
```
--scan finds every env file under a folder and skips examples, backups and dependency folders. With --share-identical, a key that has the same value in several projects becomes one shared item, so rotating it is one change.
## What this doesn't do
A reference in a committed file gives away a name, not a value. But once a command has a value, it's in that command's memory, and Pistachio can't control what the command does with it. Masking hides exact copies in its output, not altered ones. The security page covers where protection ends.
## Related
Block commits that contain secretsRefuse commits that add plain secrets to env files.Set up a clone or worktree without .envGet a new clone or worktree running without copying .env.

Page: fastlane and an App Store Connect key · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/guides/fastlane-app-store-connect-key.html

Guide · fastlane
# Use an App Store Connect key with fastlane
fastlane wants the path of a .p8 file. That file ends up in the repo folder, a Downloads folder or a backup, and it can sign in as your team.
By Zach ShallbetterPublished 14 November 2026Needs the command-line tool
In shortSave the .p8 as a key item, then run pst run --file ASC_KEY_PATH=shop/production/ASC_P8 -- fastlane beta. The command gets the path of a temporary file only you can read, and Pistachio deletes it when the command exits.
## Why the .p8 file lingers
The App Store Connect key is a .p8 file, and fastlane reads it from a path. So the file gets saved somewhere and stays there: in the project, in a shared folder, in a backup, sometimes in Git. Anyone who can read it can use the key. Replacing it means finding every copy.
The tool needs a file, not a value in the environment. Pistachio stores the key as an item in iCloud Keychain and writes a file only for the length of the command. Your project folder never holds it, and neither does a backup of that folder.
## Set it up
### Save the key as a key item
Use the key kind, the one meant for SSH, GPG, .p8 and .pem files. The value is read from standard input. The file name below is an example.
Terminal
```
pst set shop/production/ASC_P8 --kind key < ~/Downloads/AuthKey_EXAMPLE.p8
```
Saving asks for approval. Once the item is stored, delete the downloaded file. Key items are masked in command output, line by line, and only exact copies are hidden.
### Run fastlane with --file
NAME=ID sets the variable NAME to the path of a temporary file holding the item's value. Use the name your lane reads for the key's path.
Terminal
```
pst run --file ASC_KEY_PATH=shop/production/ASC_P8 -- fastlane beta
```
The file is readable only by you. Pistachio deletes it when the command exits. Temporary files for different item IDs get different paths, even if the final names match.
### Keep the setting in the project
If you run the lane the same way every time, put it in an env file. NAME=pistachio-file://ID does the same as --file, and the file contains no value.
.env.local
```
ASC_KEY_PATH=pistachio-file://shop/production/ASC_P8
```
Terminal
```
pst run --env-file .env.local -- fastlane beta
```
### Check before a slow run
pst check accepts the same options. It shows whether the item would be released without asking, would ask you, or is missing, and it releases nothing.
Terminal
```
pst check --file ASC_KEY_PATH=shop/production/ASC_P8
```
## With an agent
The key item asks for approval each time unless it is agent-safe or a grant covers it. Keep a production signing key out of agent-safe and grant it narrowly if you let an agent run releases. The MCP tool pistachio_run can deliver key files too. See Give coding agents API keys safely.
## What this doesn't do
- While the command runs, the file exists on disk. Malware running as you could read it in that time, and so can the command and anything it starts.
- Pistachio can't control what a command does with the file. It could copy it. Masking hides exact copies of each line of the key in output, not altered ones.
- Your lane still needs the other values it reads, such as the key ID and issuer ID. Those are separate items or plain settings.
- The original .p8 you downloaded is a plain copy until you delete it.
The key files section and the security page have more.
## Related
Give coding agents API keys without handing them overApprovals, grants, and keys an agent can use but never read.Push env vars to your deploy platformsSend one environment's values to Vercel, GitHub, Railway or Fly.
