Page: Guides: development secrets on a Mac · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/guides/

Guides
# Practical guides
Task-sized walkthroughs, each with the exact commands and what it doesn't cover.
## Env files
Keep values out of files, find duplicates, and set up new checkouts.

Page: Push credentials to a Linux server over SSH · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/guides/linux-server-credentials.html

Guide · Deploy
# Send credentials to your Linux server
A service on your own Linux server needs API keys and app passwords. Pasting them into files over ssh leaves no record of what's there, and the copy on your Mac and the one on the server drift apart.
By Zach ShallbetterPublished 18 November 2026Needs the command-line tool and the direct download
In shortGive the server a script that stores one credential from standard input, let your account run it with sudo and no password, name each Pistachio item ADAPTER.ACCOUNT, and link the environment with pst remote link ENV ssh host=… script=…. Every pst push asks you with Touch ID, then sends each value over ssh on standard input.
## How it works
The values stay in your Mac's keychain, where you can see, rotate and audit them. The server keeps its own copy, one root-only file per credential, which the service loads at start, for example with systemd's LoadCredential=. Pistachio's job is the delivery: it runs your server's script once per item, over your own ssh connection and keys, with the value on standard input, so it never appears in a command line, an environment variable or your shell history.
The service never talks to Pistachio, and keeps running with its last values while your Mac is off.
## Set it up
### Give the server a credential script
Pistachio runs it as sudo -n bash SCRIPT ADAPTER ACCOUNT --stdin and sends the value followed by one newline. The script must read at most 64 KiB, strip that one newline, store the value, and print stored ADAPTER.ACCOUNT when it has; anything else counts as a failure. A minimal one, with myapp as the example service:
/srv/myapp/add-credential.sh
```
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
[[ $# -eq 3 && $3 == --stdin && ! -t 0 ]] || { echo "usage: add-credential.sh ADAPTER ACCOUNT --stdin" >&2; exit 64; }
name="$1.$2"
[[ $name =~ ^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_-]*\.[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]*$ ]] || { echo "bad name" >&2; exit 64; }
value=$(head -c 65536; printf x); value=${value%x}; value=${value%$'\n'}
[[ -n $value ]] || { echo "empty value" >&2; exit 1; }
dir=/etc/myapp/credentials
umask 077
tmp=$(mktemp "$dir/.$name.XXXXXX")
printf %s "$value" > "$tmp" && mv "$tmp" "$dir/$name"
systemctl restart myapp
echo "stored $name"
```
Point the service at those files, for example with a LoadCredential=NAME:/etc/myapp/credentials/NAME line for each credential in its unit, so it reads them from $CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY.
### Let your account run it without a password
A push has no terminal, so sudo can't ask for one. Allow exactly that script, and check from your Mac:
/etc/sudoers.d/myapp-credentials
```
you ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/bash /srv/myapp/add-credential.sh *
```
Your Mac
```
ssh myserver sudo -n -l bash /srv/myapp/add-credential.sh
```
It prints the command when the rule is in place. myserver is the host as named in your SSH config.
### Store each credential under its name
Name items ADAPTER.ACCOUNT: Pistachio splits at the first dot. Both parts start with a letter or digit and use letters, digits, _ and -; the account may also contain dots.
Terminal
```
pst set myapp/production/bluesky.someone.bsky.social --kind token
```
You're asked for the value without it being shown, and saving asks for Touch ID.
### Link the environment to the server
Terminal
```
pst remote link myapp/production ssh host=myserver script=/srv/myapp/add-credential.sh
```
Linking asks once. The host and script may hold only characters a shell reads literally, and a link synced from another Mac is checked again before each push.
### Push, and approve with Touch ID
Terminal
```
pst push myapp/production --only myapp/production/bluesky.someone.bsky.social
```
The approval panel names the server, the script and every item. A server counts as production, because its script restarts the service, so tick I mean to change production, then touch the sensor. Each credential the server confirms prints as pushed.
## Keep it current
Change a value in Pistachio and push again; the script replaces the file and restarts the service. pst remote status myapp/production lists items never pushed to the server and items changed since they were. The server can't list what it holds, so that comes from Pistachio's own record of what it pushed, not from the server.
## What this doesn't do
- It doesn't remove credentials from the server. Unlinking stops future pushes; deleting a file on the server is yours to do.
- The server keeps plain-text copies, readable by root. Protect the server as you would any place that holds them.
- Each push waits for your approval on your Mac, so a script or agent can start one but can't finish it without you. Agents have no push tool.
- It's in the direct download only: the Mac App Store version can't run ssh. One value is at most 64 KiB, and empty values aren't sent.
The script contract has every rule in one place, and Push env vars to your deploy platforms covers Vercel, GitHub, Railway and Fly.
## Related
Push env vars to your deploy platformsSend one environment's values to Vercel, GitHub, Railway or Fly.Use your secrets on another Mac over SSHApprove on your own Mac what a command on another one asks for.

Page: How to keep API keys out of MCP server configs · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/guides/mcp-server-api-keys.html

Guide · MCP servers
# Keep API keys out of MCP server configs
MCP clients start servers from a JSON config, and the usual way to give a server its key is to type the key into that file. Pistachio lets the config hold a reference instead.
By Zach ShallbetterPublished 14 November 2026Needs the command-line tool
In shortSave the key in Pistachio, then change the server's command to pistachio run --no-masking -- … and put pistachio://NAME in its env. The client starts the server as before; Pistachio fills the key in for that process.
## Why the config is a problem
A config such as .mcp.json or Claude Desktop's settings file holds every server's keys in plain text. It gets shared to set up a teammate, checked into a repository for a project's tools, or synced between Macs, and every key in it goes along.
## Wrap the server
### Save the key in Pistachio
Terminal
```
pst set SOME_API_KEY --kind token
```
The value is read from a hidden prompt or standard input, so it never appears in your shell history.
### Start the server through pistachio run
MCP server config
```
{
  "command": "pistachio",
  "args": ["run", "--no-masking", "--", "npx", "-y", "some-mcp-server"],
  "env": { "SOME_API_KEY": "pistachio://SOME_API_KEY" }
}
```
--no-masking matters here: MCP speaks over standard output, which must pass through untouched.
### Decide how it may read the key
The server is started by your agent, so its reads come from the agent's process chain. Either mark the item agent-safe, or grant it for the time you'll be working; otherwise each start asks you.
Terminal
```
pst update SOME_API_KEY --agent-safe yes
```
## Pistachio's own MCP server
Terminal
```
claude mcp add pistachio -- ~/.local/bin/pistachio mcp
```
For clients without a shell, Pistachio's server offers status, listing, checking, running commands with references filled in, and asking you for a grant. It has no tool that reads a value, and the output it returns is masked.
## What this doesn't do
Only servers started as a command can be wrapped. A server reached over HTTP with a header key can't get it this way. And like any command, a wrapped server holds the key in memory once it starts.
## Related
Give coding agents API keys without handing them overApprovals, grants, and keys an agent can use but never read.Hide your OpenAI or Anthropic key from an AI agentLet a command call OpenAI or Anthropic without holding the key.

Page: Update a .env file without overwriting it · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/guides/merge-into-an-existing-env-file.html

Guide · Merge
# Merge into an existing .env file
You have a .env with your own comments and settings, and you want to add the project's variables to it. Writing a fresh file would throw all of that away.
By Zach ShallbetterPublished 14 November 2026Needs the command-line tool
In shortRun pst export shop/development --out .env.local --merge. Pistachio lists the names it will add and update, asks to go ahead, and leaves every other byte of the file as it is. --replace rewrites the whole file instead.
## Why a plain export is careful
An env file collects things over time: notes to yourself, a variable you added for one experiment, blank lines that group sections. A tool that regenerates the file removes all of it. So pst export does not overwrite an existing file. It leaves the file alone and names the variables that would change.
The examples use an example project called shop.
## Merge the variables
### See what would change
Terminal
```
pst export shop/development --out .env.local
```
With the file already there and no flag, nothing is written. Pistachio names the variables that would change, so you can decide before anything moves.
### Merge
Terminal
```
pst export shop/development --out .env.local --merge
```
It updates the variables the environment's record has, appends the ones the file is missing, and lists the names it will add and update. Then it asks to go ahead. Given this file:
.env.local, before
```
# Stripe, test mode
STRIPE_KEY=example-only

# my own notes
DEBUG_SQL=1
```
the result keeps the comments, the blank line, the order and DEBUG_SQL:
.env.local, after
```
# Stripe, test mode
STRIPE_KEY=pistachio://shop/development/STRIPE_KEY

# my own notes
DEBUG_SQL=1
DATABASE_URL=pistachio://shop/development/DATABASE_URL
```
A variable that already holds the right value is left as written. An updated line keeps its indentation and any export prefix, but loses an inline comment. Line endings and a last line without a newline are kept. If there is nothing to change, nothing is written.
### Skip the question in a script
Terminal
```
pst export shop/development --out .env.local --merge --yes
```
--yes skips the confirmation. Without a terminal it is required.
### Or replace the file
Terminal
```
pst export shop/development --out .env.local --replace
```
--replace rewrites the whole file and loses its comments and other variables. Use it when you want the file to match the record exactly.
## In the app
Choose Edit › Export Environment… on an item, or right-click a project and choose Export Environment. Pick references or values and a file. If the file exists, the sheet offers Merge, which lists the names it adds and updates before you press it, or Replace the file. It runs the same checks as the command.
## Merging values
With --values the file gets real values, in plain text. That asks for approval every time, naming the file, and refuses a file inside a Git checkout unless it is ignored and untracked. A variable already in the file is listed as an update before its value is known, and a merged file becomes readable only by you. Paste env vars into a dashboard is the option that avoids a file.
## What this doesn't do
- The file must be UTF-8 KEY=VALUE lines.
- It never removes a variable. Ones Pistachio does not manage stay, including ones you no longer want.
- If the file changes while the question waits, the merge is refused. Run it again.
- A symbolic link, or anything but a regular file, at the destination is refused.
- A file that does not exist yet is created, as without --merge.
The export reference lists every flag. For new clones, see Set up a clone or worktree without .env.
## Related
Set up a clone or worktree without .envGet a new clone or worktree running without copying .env.Paste env vars into a dashboard, no filePaste an environment into a hosting dashboard, no file on disk.

Page: Copy env vars to a dashboard without a file · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/guides/paste-env-into-a-dashboard.html

Guide · Dashboards
# Paste env vars into a dashboard, no file
Hosting dashboards let you paste a whole env block. The usual route is to save the values to a file, open it, copy it and forget to delete it. You can skip the file.
By Zach ShallbetterPublished 14 November 2026Needs the command-line tool
In shortRun pst export shop/production --values --clipboard. Approve it, paste into the dashboard, and the copy clears itself after 60 seconds. In the app, use Copy Environment as .env…. No file is written.
## Why a file is the wrong middle step
A plain-text .env.production holds every value in the open. It sits in your folder, in backups and in cloud-synced directories until you remember to delete it. The dashboard only needs the text once.
The examples use an example project called shop with a production environment.
## Copy and paste
### Copy the environment
Terminal
```
pst export shop/production --values --clipboard
```
Pistachio builds the env block from the environment's record: its stored values and its plain settings. It asks for approval every time, naming the environment and saying the values go to the clipboard. No grant, agent-safe setting or earlier approval stands in for that.
### Paste it into the dashboard
The block has no header comment, so it pastes as a clean list of NAME=value lines. Use it in any dashboard that takes a pasted env block, such as Vercel, Railway, Netlify or Render.
### Let it clear
The copy stays on this Mac. It does not travel by Universal Clipboard. It is marked concealed and transient so clipboard managers skip it, and it is cleared after 60 seconds if nothing else was copied in the meantime. A detached pistachio clipboard-clear does the clearing, so the command can exit straight away. If you copy something else first, Pistachio leaves your new copy alone.
## The same thing in the app
Open an item in the environment, then choose Edit › Copy Environment as .env…. The approval names the environment, the clipboard and when it clears. The clear time is 60 seconds unless you changed it in Settings › Privacy & Approval, where you can pick 15, 30, 60 or 120 seconds.
## When you want a file or a push instead
If you do need a file, --values --out FILE writes one readable only by you. Inside a Git checkout the file must be ignored and untracked, or nothing is asked or written. A file in a folder that syncs to iCloud Drive, Dropbox, Google Drive or OneDrive gets a warning, because the values would leave the Mac.
Terminal
```
pst export shop/production --values --out .env.production.local
```
If the environment is linked to Vercel, GitHub, Railway or Fly, pst push shop/production sends the values directly. It asks every time, and production needs its own confirmation in the app. See Push to deployment platforms.
## What this doesn't do
- A copy cannot be traced afterwards. The access log records "copied to the clipboard", never the values or where they went.
- Once pasted, the values live in the dashboard, outside Pistachio.
- Agents, Pistachio for Safari and requests forwarded over SSH cannot copy, (over SSH the clipboard would be on the other computer).
- Unconfirmed variables are noted on standard error; a reference to a missing item stops the copy.
The security page describes where protection ends, and the export reference lists every flag.
## Related
Merge into an existing .env fileAdd variables to a .env and keep your comments and order.Keep API keys out of your .env filesMove values into iCloud Keychain and leave references in the file.

Page: Stop committing secrets in env files · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/guides/pre-commit-secret-check.html

Guide · Pre-commit
# Block commits that contain secrets
One pasted key in a staged env file is enough. A pre-commit check looks at what you are about to commit and stops it before it reaches your history.
By Zach ShallbetterPublished 14 November 2026Needs the command-line tool
In shortRun pst scan --install-hook once in the repository. From then on, git commit runs pst scan --staged and refuses the commit if an added env file line holds a stored value or something that looks secret. The output names the file and line, never the value.
## Why secrets get committed
Git keeps out an env file only when your ignore rules name it. A new file name, such as .env.staging, or a file added with git add -f goes straight in. Once a key is in history, deleting the line later does not remove it from earlier commits.
A check at commit time is the cheapest place to catch this. It runs on your Mac, before anything is pushed.
## Set up the check
### Scan the folder you are in
Run the scan once by hand to see what it reports.
Terminal
```
pst scan
```
It looks for env files under the current folder: .env, .env.* and *.env. It skips examples, templates, backups, and anything in node_modules, build or .git folders. Each finding is printed as FILE:LINE NAME followed by the reason, never a value:
Terminal (example)
```
.env.staging:3  STRIPE_KEY  holds the value of shop/staging/STRIPE_KEY
```
There are two reasons. The value equals an item you have stored, or it looks secret: a private key, a connection string with credentials, a token with a known prefix such as sk_live_ or ghp_, or a value of 8 or more characters under a name like *_TOKEN, *_SECRET or *_API_KEY. Identifiers, hosts and pistachio:// references are not findings.
### Move what it found into Keychain
Import the file and rewrite it, so the value is replaced by a reference.
Terminal
```
pst import .env.staging --rewrite
```
Lines it moved are now references, so they no longer count. Keep API keys out of your .env files covers the import in full.
### Install the hook
Terminal
```
pst scan --install-hook
```
This writes a pre-commit hook that runs pistachio scan --staged. It honours core.hooksPath and works in worktrees. If the repository already has a hook that is not Pistachio's, it is left alone. Add --force to replace it.
### Commit as usual
--staged reads only the lines a commit would add, from the Git index, in env files that are staged. If it finds a plain value, the commit is refused and the file, line and variable name are given, plus the stored item when the value equals one. Fix the file and commit again. To skip the check for one commit, use git commit --no-verify.
## Use the same check in a script
pst scan exits 1 when it finds anything, so you can call it from your own script. --json prints place, key, reason (stored or looks-secret) and items for each finding.
Terminal
```
pst scan --json
```
The comparison with stored items asks for approval every time. Grants and agent-safe settings do not stand in for it, and agents cannot ask. If Pistachio can't be reached or you don't approve the comparison, values that look secret are still reported, and the exit status is 1, so the hook refuses the commit even when nothing looks secret.
## What this doesn't do
- It reads env files only. A key pasted into source code, a README or a config file is not checked.
- The "looks secret" test is a heuristic. A secret with an unusual shape under an innocent name can pass.
- Stored values shorter than 8 characters, and items saved as plain values, are left out of the comparison with Keychain.
- If neither pst nor pistachio is on the PATH, the hook says so and lets the commit through.
- git commit --no-verify skips it, as it skips any hook.
The CLI reference lists every option, and the security page explains where protection ends.
## Related
Keep API keys out of your .env filesMove values into iCloud Keychain and leave references in the file.Find the same API key in many projectsFind reused keys and give production its own.

Page: Hide an OpenAI or Anthropic key from an agent · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/guides/proxy-api-keys-for-agents.html

Guide · Key proxy
# Hide your OpenAI or Anthropic key from an AI agent
Your tests call OpenAI or Anthropic, so the agent that runs them needs a working key. It doesn't need to hold the key, and what it holds it can print.
By Zach ShallbetterPublished 14 November 2026Needs the command-line tool
In shortRun the command as pst run --proxy --env-file .env.local -- npm test. It gets a placeholder and a local base URL instead of the key, and Pistachio adds the real key only to requests bound for the provider. Add --proxy-models and --proxy-requests to narrow what it can do.
## Why a working key means an exposed key
Normally pst run puts the real value in the command's environment. That is how process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY works. It also means the command, and any agent driving it, can print the value, write it to a file or send it somewhere. Masking hides exact copies in the output, nothing more.
For OpenAI and Anthropic keys there is a better arrangement. The command doesn't need the key. It needs to make API calls that carry it. So Pistachio adds the key to those calls outside the command.
## Run the command through the proxy
### Keep the key as a whole reference
The variable must be exactly a pistachio:// reference to the key, in an env file or in the environment's record. If you haven't moved your keys yet, start with Keep API keys out of your .env files.
.env.local
```
OPENAI_API_KEY=pistachio://shop/development/OPENAI_API_KEY
```
### Add --proxy
Terminal
```
pst run --proxy --env-file .env.local -- npm test
```
The command gets a random placeholder in OPENAI_API_KEY, and OPENAI_BASE_URL points at a port on this Mac that pst run listens on. The same applies to ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL. Requests that carry the placeholder go to api.openai.com or api.anthropic.com with the real key in its place. Anything else is refused. Programs that use the OpenAI or Anthropic SDKs, or read those base URL variables, work without changes.
### Narrow what the command may do
The proxy lets the command use the key. These two options limit how.
Terminal
```
pst run --proxy --proxy-models gpt-4o-mini --proxy-requests 100 --env-file .env.local -- npm test
```
--proxy-models A,B forwards only requests whose JSON body names a listed model. A request with no body, a compressed or malformed body, or a call such as GET /v1/models is refused. --proxy-requests N refuses requests after N have been forwarded, across both providers. When either is set, pst run prints pistachio: proxy limits enforced: ... on standard error, so you can see it took effect. Both need --proxy.
### Use it from an agent that has no shell
The MCP tool pistachio_run takes the same settings as fields: proxy: true, proxy_models as an array of model names, and proxy_requests as a number. Both limits need proxy: true. The MCP guide covers adding the server.
## Who can use the proxy
Only the command and the processes it starts. A request from any other program gets a 403, even from one that read the placeholder out of the environment, and the proxy stops when the command exits. A process that detaches from the command and is adopted by launchd is refused too. The placeholder is new for each run.
## What this doesn't do
- The command and everything it starts can still use the key within your limits. It can send any prompt or file to the provider. Without --proxy-models it isn't restricted to certain paths or methods.
- Spend is capped by --proxy-requests only, not by tokens or money.
- The placeholder can show up in output or logs. It is useless outside the command's process tree, but it isn't concealed.
- Proxy mode refuses to start if a supported key isn't a whole reference, if its base URL is already set, or if the key would also reach the command through another variable or key file. At least one supported key reference is required.
- Other credentials are delivered normally. A database URL in the same run is not protected by this proxy.
- A program running as you that can attach a debugger to the command or read its memory gets whatever the command has.
See the CLI reference and the security page for the details.
## Related
Give coding agents API keys without handing them overApprovals, grants, and keys an agent can use but never read.Keep API keys out of MCP server configsStart the server through pistachio run so the config holds references.

Page: Push env vars to Vercel, GitHub and more · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/guides/push-to-deployment-platforms.html

Guide · Deploy
# Push env vars to your deploy platforms
Your keys live in one place on your Mac and in a dashboard for each service that runs your code. Every change means pasting the same value again, and nobody remembers which copy is stale.
By Zach ShallbetterPublished 14 November 2026Needs the command-line tool
In shortLink an environment once with pst remote link, check it with pst remote status, and send it with pst push. Every push asks you to approve it, and nothing is deployed: new values apply on the service's next deploy.
## Why the copies drift
A deployed app can't read your keychain, so each platform keeps its own copy of every value. Vercel has one, GitHub Actions has another, Railway and Fly have more. You change a key on your Mac, paste it into one dashboard, and forget the other two. Weeks later a build fails and nothing says which copy is old.
Pistachio can hold the list of places an environment goes. It then compares names and sends values from one place.
## Push an environment
The examples use a project called shop with a production environment. Install and sign in to the tool for each service you use first: vercel login, gh auth login, railway login or flyctl auth login. By default Pistachio runs those tools as you and stores no service tokens.
### Link the environment
Each link names a service and the target on it. Linking asks for approval. A link covers the whole environment, including items you add later.
Terminal
```
pst remote link shop/vercel.preview vercel project=shop environment=preview
pst remote link shop/production github repo=me/shop environment=production
pst remote link shop/production fly app=shop-api
```
In the app, open an item's Edit menu, choose Remote Locations…, then Add a Location…. The sheet asks for the service's details and says whether its command-line tool is installed. Add Location turns on once the details are complete. It never asks for a service token.
### Check what differs
Status shows names missing on each side, and items whose value changed since they were last pushed. It compares names and doesn't use values.
Terminal
```
pst remote status shop/production
```
### Rehearse, then push
Use --dry-run for a first look before a real push. Then run the push. You can limit it to one link with --to or to chosen items with --only.
Terminal
```
pst push shop/production --dry-run
pst push shop/production
pst push shop/production --to LINK_ID --only shop/production/DATABASE_URL
```
Every push asks, every time, and no grant covers one. A production target also needs I mean to change production ticked in the approval panel. The Pistachio app does the pushing, so it must be running; pst push asks it. With a command-line tool, values reach the tool on standard input, never as arguments. Find a link's ID for --to with pst remote list shop/production.
### See what changed since the last push
After a push, Pistachio records when each item went to each link. An item changed since then gets an orange badge in the list and "Changed since last push" in its detail. Review has a Changes filter that lists those items, and also items not pushed yet, with a Push… action.
## Push through an API instead
If you'd rather not depend on the command-line tools, keep the service's access token as an ordinary Pistachio item and name it in the link. Use a token limited to what you push.
Terminal
```
pst set VERCEL_TOKEN --kind token
pst remote link shop/vercel.preview vercel project=shop environment=preview token=VERCEL_TOKEN
```
The Mac App Store version can only push this way, and it can't push to GitHub. The CLI reference lists every key each service takes.
## A service on a Linux server
A service on your own Linux server can read its credentials from files, for example a systemd unit with LoadCredential=. Give the server a script that stores one credential from standard input, and link the environment to it over ssh. Name each item ADAPTER.ACCOUNT:
Terminal
```
pst set distribution/production/bluesky.someone.bsky.social --kind token
pst remote link distribution/production ssh host=myserver script=/srv/app/add-credential.sh
pst push distribution/production
```
Pistachio runs sudo -n bash SCRIPT ADAPTER ACCOUNT --stdin on the server once per item, with your SSH keys and the value on standard input, and counts it as pushed only when the script prints stored ADAPTER.ACCOUNT. Your account needs a sudoers rule to run that script without a password. Every push to a server counts as production, since the script restarts the service. The script contract has the details; the direct download only.
## What this doesn't do
- It deploys nothing. Railway and Fly would deploy by default, so Pistachio turns that off. New values take effect on the service's next deploy, which you start.
- Unlinking stops tracking and pushing. Values already at the service stay there, on a Linux server too: Pistachio can't remove a credential the script stored.
- Pushing Fly secrets through flyctl sends one line per value, so multi-line values aren't supported on that route. When you push through an API token, variable names must be letters, digits and underscores, and GitHub refuses names starting with GITHUB_.
- Pistachio records what it sent, not what a service later does with it. A push always waits for your approval, so a script or agent can start one but can't complete it without you. Agents have no push tool.
## Related
Paste env vars into a dashboard, no filePaste an environment into a hosting dashboard, no file on disk.Rotate the keys an AI agent touchedList what an agent was given, then replace each key in one pass.

Page: Rotate the keys an AI agent touched · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/guides/rotate-after-an-agent-session.html

Guide · Rotation
# Rotate the keys an AI agent touched
After a long agent session you can't say for sure which keys it ran with. Pistachio keeps a log of every release, so you can list those keys and replace them instead of guessing.
By Zach ShallbetterPublished 14 November 2026Needs the command-line tool
In shortRun pst touched --since 4h --by claude to list the items Pistachio released to programs under claude. Then run pst rotate --touched --since 4h --by claude --open --push to replace each one, end the grants that covered it and push the new value to linked environments.
## Why you end up rotating everything
An agent runs commands for you, and those commands need keys. Once a command has a value, it is in that command's memory and environment. Masking hides exact copies in the output, but it can't stop a command that prints, sends or encodes the value in another form. So after a session you can't prove which keys stayed private.
The usual answer is to rotate every key in the project. That is slow, and people skip it. A better answer is to rotate only what the agent could have seen, and to have a list of that. Pistachio writes one entry to its access log for each release, with the program chain, folder and command. It never logs values. The list comes from that log.
For the setup that comes before the session, see Give coding agents API keys safely.
## List the keys, then replace them
### See what was released
pst touched lists the items released to commands in a time window, including through pst run. --by claude narrows it to programs running under claude, so keys you read yourself in the same hours don't show up. Use the same window you worked in.
Terminal
```
pst touched --since 4h --by claude
```
Without --by you get every release in that time, to anything. If you worked under a single grant, --grant ID lists what that grant released. Add --json for scripts.
### Replace them with one command
Give pst rotate the same filters and it works through the same list, one item at a time. Add --open to open the service's key page where Pistachio knows it, and --push to send the new values to the environments you linked.
Terminal
```
pst rotate --touched --since 4h --by claude --open --push
```
First it ends any grant that covers these items. Then, for each item, it shows where to make the new key and asks for the new value; leave it empty to skip that item. You make the key in the service's dashboard and paste it in. The old value stays in the item's history. With --push, the new value then goes to each linked environment, such as a Vercel project. A push asks every time, and production needs its own confirmation in the app.
### Rotate one key by name
You can also name items or use a pattern. This is useful when the list shows one key that matters more than the rest.
Terminal
```
pst rotate shop/development/STRIPE_KEY --open --push
```
### Check Activity
Open Activity in the Pistachio app to see the same releases with more detail. An entry shows the action, the items, the decision, who asked through which programs, the folder and the command. You can filter by event and project.
## Shorten the list next time
The smaller the grant, the shorter the list. A grant can end when the agent quits (--session), cover one command (--command) or last one use (--once). Keys behind --proxy never reach the command, so you can leave them out of the rotation, though they still appear in the list because pst run itself fetched them. The proxy guide covers that.
## What this doesn't do
- It can't make the new key. Stripe, GitHub, OpenAI and most services only issue keys in their dashboards. Pistachio takes you to the page and saves what you paste.
- touched reads Pistachio's access log for values released to commands. It says nothing about what a command did with a value.
- Values copied or written with pst export --values, filled by Safari or shown from history are logged but not listed by touched; check Activity for those.
- Rotation replaces the stored value and ends grants. It does not recall a value that was already released, and it does not disable the old key at the service. Do that in the service.
- History keeps old values, with your approval to read them, for up to 30 days after deletion or until they are more than 10 versions old. Use Forget History when an old value shouldn't linger.
The CLI reference has the full option list, and the security page says where protection ends.
## Related
Give coding agents API keys without handing them overApprovals, grants, and keys an agent can use but never read.Hide your OpenAI or Anthropic key from an AI agentLet a command call OpenAI or Anthropic without holding the key.

Page: Save an API key from Safari to Pistachio · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/guides/save-keys-from-safari.html

Guide · Safari
# Save an API key straight from the provider's page
A provider shows you a new key once. You copy it, paste it somewhere to keep it, and hope the clipboard and that somewhere stay private.
By Zach ShallbetterPublished 14 November 2026
In shortTurn on Pistachio for Safari. When a page shows a new key, press Save to Pistachio, name it, and approve. Later, the extension can fill it into a key field on the right site after you approve with Touch ID.
## Why new keys end up in the wrong places
Most services only issue keys in their dashboards, and show the value once. The fast path is copy, paste into a note or a chat, then into an env file. Each stop is another copy of a secret, and some of them sync or get backed up.
Pistachio for Safari recognises the key on the page and keeps the value in the page until you press Save, when it goes to the app. Spotting happens in the page.
## Save a key
### Turn the extension on
Open Safari, then Settings, then Extensions, and enable Pistachio. Safari asks you to allow it on each site, or on all of them. Its toolbar button says whether it can reach Pistachio and lists what it found on the page. Use Safari's website permissions to choose which sites it may inspect.
### Make the key at the provider
Go to the provider's key page and create the key. The extension knows about twenty or so providers, including Stripe, OpenAI, Anthropic, GitHub and npm. It also catches private keys, database URLs that contain a password, and long random values labelled as a secret or token. It skips masked values, examples, Stripe and PostHog public keys, and bare hashes.
When the page says it won't show the key again, the save panel opens by itself, once. Otherwise a Save to Pistachio button appears on the box holding the key, for strong matches.
### Choose a place and a name
The panel opens beside the key, not over it. Choose where it goes, either shared or a project's environment, and give it a name. A live or test key is matched to production or development when it can be. Press Save to Pistachio.
### Approve and copy the reference
The app asks you to approve, and shows the page's site. After the save, the panel shows the pistachio:// reference, ready to copy, and a new item's note says where it came from. Saving over an existing item keeps the old value in its history.
Example reference
```
STRIPE_KEY=pistachio://shop/development/STRIPE_KEY
```
### Fill it back in later
Click into a field that expects a key, token or secret, and a Pistachio badge appears in it. Pick an item from the list, approve with Touch ID, and the value goes into that field. Fill asks every time.
## If it missed the key
Select the text, Control-click, and choose Save Selection to Pistachio. Less certain finds aren't marked on the page. The toolbar button shows a count, and its panel lists them with a short preview, never the value.
## What this doesn't do
- Fill works only on the item's own service site, such as dashboard.stripe.com for a Stripe key, and on deployment dashboards such as Vercel, GitHub, Railway and Fly. It never fills on sites a platform hosts for customers, such as vercel.app. You can set the sites per item with Fill in Safari on; the list replaces the default.
- Fill works over https only and never inside a frame. No grant or agent-safe setting replaces the approval.
- Detection covers the main page, not embedded frames or shadow roots, and it depends on the permissions you gave and on supported patterns. Password fields aren't read.
- The extension can't read stored values. The one exception is fill, after you approve it.
See what the extension can and can't reach. To use the saved key in a project, keep references in your env files.
## Related
Keep API keys out of your .env filesMove values into iCloud Keychain and leave references in the file.Find the same API key in many projectsFind reused keys and give production its own.

Page: Use local secrets on a Mac over SSH · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/guides/secrets-over-ssh.html

Guide · SSH
# Use your secrets on another Mac over SSH
You work on a second Mac through SSH and its commands need keys that live on your laptop. Copying a .env file across leaves a plain-text copy behind.
By Zach ShallbetterPublished 14 November 2026Needs the command-line tool
In shortConnect with ssh -R to forward Pistachio's socket, set PISTACHIO_SOCKET on the other Mac, and run pistachio run there. The request reaches the app on your own Mac, which asks you to approve each read of an item that needs approval.
## Why files are the wrong answer
A remote shell has no Touch ID and no keychain of yours. The usual fixes are to copy the env file over, or to paste values into the session. Both leave the values in a file or in shell history on a machine you may not control as tightly as your laptop.
Pistachio's command-line tool never touches the keychain. It asks the app over a Unix socket. If you forward that socket over SSH, the tool on the far Mac asks the app on your Mac, and the approval appears where you are sitting.
## Set it up
Your Mac needs the Pistachio app running; the other Mac needs the pistachio tool, which is macOS only. Forwarding needs the direct-download app on your Mac: the Mac App Store version doesn't support it yet. If the other Mac has the App Store version installed, set PISTACHIO_BROKER=direct there too. $USER expands to your login name on each Mac: use the same name on both, or put a fixed name in both commands.
### Forward the socket when you connect
Run this on your own Mac, with the Pistachio app running. devmac is an example host name.
Your Mac
```
ssh -o StreamLocalBindUnlink=yes \
  -R /tmp/pistachio-$USER.sock:"$HOME/Library/Application Support/Latchkey/broker.sock" \
  devmac
```
### Point the tool at the forwarded socket
In that SSH session, on the other Mac, set PISTACHIO_SOCKET to the path you forwarded to.
The other Mac
```
export PISTACHIO_SOCKET=/tmp/pistachio-$USER.sock
```
### Run your command
Use pistachio run as you would at home. Here shop/development is an example environment.
The other Mac
```
pistachio run --env shop/development -- npm test
```
### Approve on your Mac
The approval panel opens on your own Mac. It says the request came over SSH and shows what the tool on the other computer says it is running, marked as unchecked. Approve with Touch ID, or deny. A request nobody answers is denied after two minutes.
## What is different from working locally
- Each read asks, unless the item is set to need no approval. Your Mac sees only your ssh client, not the program on the other computer, so grants don't apply and can't be made over the connection.
- pistachio status on the other Mac says it can't check the app's signature through a forwarded socket.
- Copying to the clipboard is refused over SSH, because the clipboard would be on the other computer.
The Agents and MCP reference has the same setup in short form, and Security explains how Pistachio identifies callers.
## What this doesn't do
- It doesn't sync secrets to the other Mac. Nothing is stored there: the value goes to the command you run. Syncing items to a second Mac through iCloud Keychain is a separate feature, and its second-Mac test is still pending.
- The forwarded socket on the other computer is created owner-only, using sshd's default StreamLocalBindMask. Anyone with your account there can use it while you are connected.
- Your Mac can't verify the far side. The program name in the panel is only what the tool reports. Read the command, and deny what you don't recognise.
- Once a command has a value, Pistachio can't control what that command does with it.
## Related
Give coding agents API keys without handing them overApprovals, grants, and keys an agent can use but never read.See which programs read your secretsSee which programs read which secrets, and check the log is intact.

Page: Temporary AWS credentials for local commands · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/guides/short-lived-aws-credentials.html

Guide · AWS
# Use short-lived AWS credentials locally
A long-lived AWS access key in your shell or an env file works until someone deletes it. A command that only needs to run for a few minutes should get credentials that stop working on their own.
By Zach ShallbetterPublished 14 November 2026Needs the command-line tool
In shortRun pst run --aws-session --env shop/development -- terraform plan. Pistachio signs a request to AWS STS with your stored access key and gives the command the temporary credentials that come back, valid for 15 minutes by default. Add --aws-role ARN to assume a role instead.
## Why the long-lived key is the problem
Put a long-lived access key in ~/.zshrc, a .env file or a CI log and it keeps working, for anyone who has a copy, until you rotate it. Most local commands, a Terraform plan or a deploy script, run for minutes. A credential that outlives them is more than they need.
The alternative is temporary credentials from AWS STS. Pistachio requests them for you and hands them to one command, so the long-lived key can stay in iCloud Keychain. Each run gets a fresh set, so there is nothing to refresh by hand and nothing to clean up afterwards.
## Set it up
### Store the long-lived key as references
The two halves of your access key are items in an environment, referenced by the names AWS tools look for. Import them from an env file, or save each one with pst set. Both variables must be pistachio:// references.
.env.local
```
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=pistachio://shop/development/AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=pistachio://shop/development/AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
```
### Ask for a session
Terminal
```
pst run --aws-session --env shop/development -- terraform plan
```
Pistachio signs a request to AWS STS with the stored key. The command receives AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_SESSION_TOKEN and AWS_CREDENTIAL_EXPIRATION. The long-lived key never reaches it. You don't need the AWS CLI installed.
### Assume a role instead
Pass --aws-role with the role's ARN to get that role's credentials. The ARN below is an example.
Terminal
```
pst run --aws-role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/dev --env shop/development -- terraform plan
```
### Pick how long it lasts
The credentials last 15 minutes unless --aws-for says otherwise, from 15 minutes to 12 hours; a shorter time is raised to 15 minutes. A role's own maximum session duration still applies, and AWS refuses a longer request. Use the shortest time that covers the command.
Terminal
```
pst run --aws-role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/dev --aws-for 1h --env shop/development -- terraform plan
```
## With an agent
An agent that runs your infrastructure commands is a good fit for this. If the credentials end up in its output, a file or a transcript, they stop working when the time is up. The long-lived key was never in the command, so there is nothing long-lived to rotate afterwards. Items that aren't agent-safe or covered by a grant ask you first, as with any other run. See Give coding agents API keys safely for approvals and grants.
## What this doesn't do
- Short-lived is not the same as narrow. The credentials can do what the key, or the role, can do until they expire. Limit the role in AWS if the command needs less.
- Without a role, the credentials come from AWS's GetSessionToken, and AWS doesn't let those call IAM operations without MFA. If the command manages IAM, assume a role with --aws-role.
- MFA isn't supported yet.
- Pistachio uses AWS's global STS endpoint, so it doesn't cover accounts in the China or GovCloud partitions.
- Within the time window, a command that holds the credentials can still print, write or send them. Masking only hides exact copies in its output.
- Pistachio doesn't change your AWS setup. The access key and the role must already exist.
The CLI reference lists the options, and the security page says where protection ends.
## Related
Rotate the keys an AI agent touchedList what an agent was given, then replace each key in one pass.Give coding agents API keys without handing them overApprovals, grants, and keys an agent can use but never read.

Page: Set up a git worktree without copying .env · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/guides/worktrees-and-fresh-clones.html

Guide · Worktrees
# Set up a clone or worktree without .env
A fresh clone or a new git worktree has no .env, because the file was never committed. Copying it from another folder spreads your keys one folder further.
By Zach ShallbetterPublished 14 November 2026Needs the command-line tool
In shortRun pst project in the new checkout to see which project it is, then either write an env file of references with pst export shop/development --out .env.local or skip the file and start the app with pst run --env shop/development -- npm run dev.
## Why the file is missing
An env file is gitignored, so it stays in the folder where you made it. git worktree add and git clone give you the tracked files only. The usual fix is to copy the old file across, and every copy is another place a key can leak from.
Pistachio keeps a record for each environment: its variables, each pointing at a stored item or holding a plain setting such as PORT=3000. The record belongs to the project, not to a folder, so a new checkout can use it. The examples below use an example project called shop.
## Set up the new checkout
### Ask which project this is
Terminal
```
cd ~/Projects/_worktrees/shop/fix-checkout
pst project
```
Pistachio matches the checkout to a project by its Git remotes, read from git's config and never with credentials. It shows the matching project, its environments, and a suggested export command.
### Link the checkout if nothing matches
Terminal
```
pst project link shop
```
This remembers the checkout's origin as project shop and asks you first. Use --remote R to name another remote. After that, a clone in any folder resolves to shop, and an import from it names items after the project rather than the folder.
### Write an env file of references
Terminal
```
pst export shop/development --out .env.local
```
The file holds pistachio:// references and plain settings, sorted by name, and no values. If the file already exists, it is left alone and the variables that would change are named. Merge into an existing .env file covers that case.
.env.local, after
```
# Pistachio environment shop/development
DATABASE_URL=pistachio://shop/development/DATABASE_URL
PORT=3000
STRIPE_KEY=pistachio://shop/development/STRIPE_KEY
```
### Or run without a file
Terminal
```
pst run --env shop/development -- npm run dev
```
--env sets the environment's variables from its record when the command starts. Nothing is written to the folder. Without a record for that environment, it loads what the older lookup finds and says so.
## Let an agent work in the worktree
If a coding agent works in the new worktree, a grant for the main repository's folder covers it. Grants cover the folder, the folders inside it and that repository's worktrees.
Terminal
```
pst grant 'shop/development/*' --folder ~/Projects/shop --for 2h
```
The grant asks once, lasts two hours here; --for always makes one that lasts until you revoke it. See Give coding agents API keys safely.
## What this doesn't do
- A project match only names the project. It never releases a value or widens a grant.
- A match through a remote other than origin, as a fork has, is flagged and never taken as the project.
- Values are still released only after approval, unless an item is agent-safe or a grant covers it.
- A file written without --values holds references, not values, so it needs Pistachio to fill them in when a command starts.
- If an environment has no record yet, pst env migrate builds one from what Pistachio already knows. Variables found through old file locations stay unconfirmed until you run pst env confirm.
See the environments and export reference.
## Related
Merge into an existing .env fileAdd variables to a .env and keep your comments and order.Give coding agents API keys without handing them overApprovals, grants, and keys an agent can use but never read.

Page: Pistachio: Your secrets. In a shell.
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/

A native Mac app by Snack Studio
# Your secrets.In a shell.
API keys and credentials, kept in Keychain. Ready for the commands and coding agents you approve.
Download for Mac See how it works
Free to use · macOS 15 or later
Design preview with example data. Try the working app demo.
Kept in Keychain. References in your files. Access you approve.
## Less copying. More building.
Import your environment once. Keep your workflow. Pistachio keeps the values in Keychain and leaves references in your project. Your commands get the credentials you approve when they start.
1
### References in your files. Values in Keychain.
Point Pistachio at an env file. A dry run shows where each value would go and sends nothing. Then one approval saves them to iCloud Keychain under the repository's name and the environment the file name implies, and --rewrite leaves a reference where each value was. Settings such as PORT are recognised and left in the file; --skip leaves out anything else you name.
Terminal
```
pst import .env.local --dry-run --skip PORT
pst import .env.local --rewrite --skip PORT
```
Importing, every option 2
### Recreate the env file in any checkout.
Project environment records sync with your credentials across your Macs. A fresh checkout or worktree shouldn't mean rebuilding your environment by hand: pst project recognizes the checkout from its Git remote, and pst export writes its env file from the record, with references and plain settings, never a value, and without relying on the original machine's file paths.
Environments, projects and export 3
### Your credentials aren't tied to one Mac.
Items, their history and each environment's record are keychain items in Pistachio's own access group, carried end to end encrypted by iCloud Keychain to every Mac signed in to your Apple Account with Pistachio installed. On the next Mac, clone and export, and the same environment is there. Grants stay on the Mac where you made them.
Second-Mac test pending Keychain sync is Apple's; we haven't yet run this whole sequence on a second Mac for the release.
How sync works, and its limits 4
### Agents run the commands. You decide what they get.
Agents can check what a task needs, run commands through Pistachio, and ask for access when a grant doesn't cover it. Set grants for a folder, a session, a command or a time limit. Review activity, and revoke the grant when the work is done. A request the grant doesn't cover, like production, asks again.
Agents, skills and MCP
## Be the person at the Mac
An agent's command is asking for two keys. Choose in the panel the way you would in the app: Deny prints the real refusal, Allow Once runs the tests with the values concealed, and a grant shows the next run going through, or, limited to one command, asking again.
You're the person at the Mac: when the agent's command asks, choose in the panel.
Everything the panel shows comes from macOS, not from the request: the program and those that started it, the folder it runs in, and its full command line. A script that talks to Pistachio directly instead of through the signed pst tool is named by its path, with a warning. The same limits can be set ahead of time with pst grant 'shop/development/*' --session --for 4h.
claude in ~/Projects/shop Claude wants to use 2 itemsClaude in ~/Projects/shop
shop/development/DATABASE_URL, shop/development/STRIPE_KEY
Details
Asked by
Claude, via zsh › claude › Terminal
Folder
~/Projects/shop
Command
pst run --env shop/development -- npm test
Allow from this folder until claude quitsfor 1 hourfor 8 hoursfor 1 dayfor 7 days Only for npm test
## Every item, grant and request in one Mac window
Items grouped by project and environment, which ones agents may read without asking, where each is used, every request in Activity, and the grants in effect. This window works with example data. What you chose in the panel above is already in its Activity, and a grant you made is under Grants, where Revoke stops future reads through it. Changes ask for Touch ID; revealing a value asks unless its No Approval setting permits it.
The Pistachio window, with example data. With scripts on, it works: search, filter by type or environment, pick a project or service in the sidebar, and open an item. It lists:
- shop: DATABASE_URL, STRIPE_KEY, PGHOST and NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL for development; DATABASE_URL for preview, not pushed yet; DATABASE_URL and STRIPE_KEY for production, the key changed since its last push
- blog: ADMIN_PASSWORD, SENTRY_DSN and GITHUB_TOKEN
- api: the ASC_P8 key file and API_BASE_URL
- Shared: OPENAI_API_KEY and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
Opening an item shows its value (hidden until Touch ID), reference, type, access, service, project, environment, note, location, history and recent activity. Review lists what may need a look.
Example data; the values are made up. The menu bar icon opens a smaller panel with search and recent activity, like the one above the terminal.
### When a key changes, the reference doesn't.
pst touched lists every key Pistachio released to programs an agent started. pst rotate walks through them: it ends the grants that cover them, opens each service's page for a new key, and saves what you paste, with the old value kept in history. Every file and environment that refers to the item keeps working; with --push, linked Vercel, GitHub Actions, Railway and Fly environments get the new value too.
Rotating
## Keep supported API keys out of agent processes
For OpenAI and Anthropic, Pistachio's local proxy keeps the upstream key out of the command while forwarding its API requests. The process can still use the provider; it never receives the original key. Try what a command could do with it:
### Try a command
Interactive example · no real keys
In the command's environment
```
OPENAI_API_KEY=lk-proxy-3f9c…8e4a
OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:52817/v1
```
Destination: api.openai.com
```
POST /v1/chat/completions
Authorization: Bearer — (no request yet)
```
```
Choose something for the command to try.
```
The command gets a placeholder and a base URL on your Mac; Pistachio adds the real key to requests bound for api.openai.com or api.anthropic.com and refuses unauthenticated ones. Other credentials are still delivered normally. For AWS, pst run --aws-session gives the command STS credentials that expire after 15 minutes, while your long-lived key stays in Pistachio.
Terminal
```
pst run --proxy --env shop/development -- npm test
pst run --aws-role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/dev -- terraform plan
```
## Works with your terminal, coding agents, deploy platforms and Safari
Terminal and CLIRun commands with values filled in, check what a run would get, and manage items, environments and history with pst. Coding agentsA skill for Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and Cursor; an MCP server with no secret-read tool; approvals and scoped grants. Deployment platformsLink an environment to Vercel, GitHub Actions, Railway or Fly, see what's missing, and push with each service's own tool. Browser and providersPistachio for Safari saves a new key from the page where you made it. The proxy covers OpenAI and Anthropic; STS covers AWS.
## What it protects, and where it stops
Values live in iCloud Keychain in an access group only the signed Pistachio app can read. The pst tool checks the app's signature before sending anything, the app reads each caller's identity from the kernel, and every release, change and refusal goes in a tamper-evident log. The limits are stated as precisely as the protections.
A released value is out of its handsA command you allowed has the key, and Pistachio can't control what it does with it. --proxy is the exception, for OpenAI and Anthropic: the command gets a placeholder, never the key. A reference isn't permissionIt names a secret; it doesn't grant access to it. A committed file of references gives away names, not values, and every read that isn't agent-safe or granted still asks. Anything running as you can askAny program in your Mac account can ask, not only agents. The panel names who asked and from where; keep grants narrow and short, and deny what you don't recognize.
The security model, trust boundaries and limits
## Free today. Pro is planned as a one-time purchase.
Everything above is free in the direct download, and will be in the Mac App Store version, with no account and no trial. Pistachio Pro adds four sets of tools on top, as a one-time in-app purchase in the Mac App Store, with updates included and no subscription.

## Price, licensing and what’s next
Is Pistachio free?
Yes. Everything Pistachio does today is free to download and use, with no account or trial. Storage, references, import, running commands, approvals, the security protections and export aren't part of Pro.
What will Pro add?
Pro is for one developer working across projects, Macs and agents: agent controls, recovery and migration, rotation and lifecycle, and provider integrations. They're planned, and none is sold before it exists. Shared team environments are Pistachio Teams, a separate product.
Can I buy Pro now?
No. Pro isn't on sale. It will be a one-time in-app purchase in the Mac App Store version, with its features stated before anyone pays. Ask to hear when it is.
Will the free download stay?
That's the plan: the direct download stays free, with everything that is free in Pistachio. Pro is only in the Mac App Store version.
Will my credentials ever depend on a license?
No. Your values stay in your iCloud Keychain, and you can always read or export them through Pistachio's approvals, whatever plan you're on.
Does Pistachio send my credentials anywhere?
Not to Pistachio: there's no Pistachio server or account. Values sync through iCloud Keychain to your own Macs, and leave them only where you send them: to a command you've allowed, or to a deployment platform you push to.
Is the source available?
Yes. Pistachio is source-available under the Functional Source License (FSL-1.1-ALv2): free to read, change and use for anything but a competing product, with each version becoming Apache 2.0 two years after release. Read it on GitHub.
When is Teams coming?
When real teams have shown they'll pay for it. We're looking for two or three design partners first; nothing is built before then.
Can you help my team move over?
Yes. The Developer Credential Migration is a fixed-scope engagement for small teams on Macs, from $2,500. See what it includes.
How do refunds and other Macs work?
Apple handles both: refunds through reportaproblem.apple.com, and Pro unlocks on the Macs signed in to your Apple Account. See the terms.

Keep your projects, credentials and coding agents working together, with access you can inspect and control. Pistachio is free to download and use, and the core is meant to stay free. Pro will add more for a one-time price in the Mac App Store.

Page: Privacy policy · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/privacy.html

# Privacy policy
Pistachio itself collects nothing about you. There is no Pistachio server, account, telemetry, analytics or advertising. Snack Studio never receives your credentials or anything about how you use them.
Effective 12 November 2026. Applies to the Pistachio app, its command-line tool, MCP server and Safari extension, and to this website.
## What stays on your Macs
- Your values are kept in your keychain: iCloud Keychain, which syncs them end to end encrypted between your own Apple devices, or this Mac's login keychain. Apple can't read iCloud Keychain contents, and neither can we.
- Item details, environment records, grants and the access log are kept in your keychain and in Pistachio's folder on your Mac. They never leave it except through iCloud Keychain sync or an export you ask for.
- Folders and files you choose are remembered on your Mac so Pistachio can rewrite them later. Removing the permission forgets them.
## When values leave your Mac
Only when you, or a command you allowed, sends them:
- Commands you run with pst run receive the values you approved, and do with them what they do.
- Deployment platforms you push to (Vercel, Railway, Fly, and, in the copy downloaded from this site, GitHub and your own Linux hosts over ssh) receive the values you push, either through their own command-line tools and your own sign-in to them, or, in the Mac App Store version and for any link where you choose a token item, in direct requests from the app to the service’s own API (api.vercel.com, backboard.railway.com, api.machines.dev, and api.github.com from the downloaded copy only) using the access token in the item you chose, which is sent only to that service. The Mac App Store version doesn’t push to GitHub. Their privacy policies apply.
- The key proxy forwards your requests to OpenAI or Anthropic with your key, when you run a command with --proxy.
- Short-lived AWS credentials are requested from AWS (sts.amazonaws.com) with your key, when you ask for them.
- The Safari extension fills or saves values on the pages you choose, after your approval.
- The clipboard: copied values stay on this Mac, are hidden from clipboard history apps, and are cleared after a short time.
## Updates
The copy of Pistachio downloaded from this site checks https://latchkey.snackstud.io/appcast.xml for new versions. That's a standard web request with Pistachio's version number; no system profile (hardware, operating system or usage details) is sent. Turn it off in Settings with Check for updates automatically, or check by hand with Check for Updates…. The Mac App Store version is updated by the App Store.
## Purchases
Pistachio Pro will be sold by Apple through the Mac App Store; it isn't on sale yet. Apple processes the payment and tells the app, on your Mac, that Pro is unlocked; we receive Apple's standard sales reports, which don't identify you. Apple's privacy policy applies to the purchase.
## Crash reports
If you share crash reports and analytics with app developers in macOS settings, Apple may pass us anonymous crash reports for Pistachio. They never contain your values.
## This website
The site uses no cookies, analytics or third-party requests: fonts are your system's, and every script is served from this site. The host keeps standard request logs (address, page, time) for operating the site. Your appearance preference and the homepage’s human/agent view choice are stored only in this browser’s local storage; they are not sent to us.
## Email
If you write to Contact support, we keep the conversation to answer you and delete it when it's no longer needed. Never send a real secret.
## Children
Pistachio is a developer tool and isn't directed at children.
## Changes and contact
Changes to this policy are published on this page with a new effective date. Pistachio is made by Snack Studio. Questions: Contact support.

Page: Roadmap: what's built and what's next · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/roadmap.html

Roadmap · November 2026
# What’s built, what’s next and what Pistachio won’t do
Pistachio keeps secrets for one person's Macs and the agents running on them. Files hold pistachio:// references; the app holds the values and releases them when a command starts. Below is what's built and what's planned, by tier, and then what Pistachio won't do.
Guiding rule: values move from the keychain straight to the process that needs them. People approve; agents get references.
- BuiltCLI: run, check, import, export, scan, duplicates, environments, grants, rotate, push, log, MCP
- BuiltMac app: window, import sheet, menu bar, settings, Pistachio for Safari
- BuiltApproval panel, then Touch ID, Apple Watch or password; grants; a tamper-evident access log
- BuiltA public, notarized release, with Homebrew and in-app updates
- PendingSync tried end to end on a second Mac
Only what's next up S smallM mediumL large
Tier 1
## Fix the basics
Things that undercut daily use or trust today.
S
### Sign the app with your team
Built
Gap: unsigned builds can't use iCloud Keychain, so nothing syncs, and every reinstall makes macOS ask for your login password per item.
Built: with DEVELOPMENT_TEAM set in App/project.yml, scripts/install.sh signs with your team and pst status reports iCloud Keychain storage. Notarization only matters for sharing builds.
- You
S
### CLI starts the app when it isn't running
Built
Gap: if the app is closed, every pistachio command fails with “cannot reach the app”.
Built: when the socket is missing, the tool launches Pistachio in the background, waits for it to answer, then carries on.
- YouAgents
M
### Time-limited grants
Built
Gap: when you step away, approval prompts time out and agents stall.
Plan: grants such as “agents in ~/Projects/site may read these 4 items for 2 hours”, created from the window or from an approval. Each grant appears in Activity and can be revoked.
- Agents
M
### “Allow for this project” on the approval
Built
Gap: the system sheet can only say yes or no, with one line of context.
Built: a Pistachio panel shows who is asking, from which folder and for which command, with Deny, Allow Once, and Allow from Folder for a set time, and reads Touch ID right in the panel. Several requests from the same agent share one panel and one touch.
- YouAgents
M
### Verify callers by code signature
Gap: the caller chain is process names, which any program can fake, and callers are identified by PID, which can be reused.
Built: the caller is identified by its audit token and checked by code signature as Pistachio's own tool or not. Next: check the signing team of each parent in the chain (Claude, Cursor, Terminal), which are still named by their files.
- Agents
Tier 1b
## Where secrets come from and where they go
Know what each key is for, notice when one leaks, and get to the right place to replace it.
M
### Origin and rotation details
Next up
Gap: an item is a name and a value. When one leaks, nothing says which service issued it or where to make a new one.
Plan: record what the Passwords app records for a login, adapted to keys: the service, account or project, the console URL where it's managed, who made it and when, when it was last rotated, and which projects use it. import and the app fill these in where they can (for example from a key's prefix: sk_live_ is Stripe, ghp_ is GitHub).
- YouAgents
L
### Leak alerts
Next up
Gap: if a key is pushed to a public repo or pasted somewhere, you find out from the provider, if at all.
Plan: read GitHub secret-scanning alerts for your repos through gh, scan your own repos and history locally (fingerprints only, values never leave the Mac), and match what's found against your items. A match marks the item compromised, notifies you, and shows where it was found.
- You
M
### Compromised: replace it in one place
Built
Gap: replacing a leaked key means remembering the console, the new value, and every project and service that used it.
Built: pst rotate ends the grants that cover an item, opens its service's page for a new key, saves what you paste with the old value in history, and pushes to linked environments with --push. pst touched lists what an agent was given.
- You
M
### Projects and environments
Built
Gap: one flat list doesn't capture that a project has development, staging and production values.
Built: IDs project/environment/NAME (pistachio://acp/production/DATABASE_URL), import placement from the repo and file name, moving items with their references, project-wide grants, and a service field filled in on import. Next: remote locations (Vercel, GitHub Actions, Fly) recorded alongside local files.
- YouAgents
L
### Remote machines and services
Built
Gap: values are needed on servers, in CI and in hosted environments, and today they're copied by hand.
Built: link an environment to Vercel, GitHub Actions, Railway or Fly; names-only status; push with approval every time and an extra confirmation for production; out-of-date tracking. Also built: forward the Pistachio socket over SSH, so a command on another Mac asks you on yours, and push credentials to a script on a Linux server over ssh. Next: agents on a Linux server that ask your Mac for values, with an identity for the server and grants it can use unattended.
- YouAgents
M
### Version history and recovery
Built
Gap: a changed or deleted value was gone, and a file rewritten to references could lose its only copy.
Built: the last 10 values of each item, Recently Deleted for 30 days, restore with approval, synced like the items.
- You
M
### Duplicates and combine
Built
Gap: the same key copied into many projects meant many places to rotate it, and production sharing a key with development.
Built: pistachio duplicates compares values inside Pistachio with one approval and recommends what to do; pistachio combine makes them one shared item, and the files follow.
- You
Tier 2
## Coding agents
Where Pistachio can be clearly better than a .env file or a password manager.
M
### Use a value without holding it
Gap: “agent-safe” means the agent can hold the value: it can call pistachio get, and masking only catches exact copies.
Plan: refuse get to agent callers, and mask base64, URL-encoded and JSON-escaped copies too.
- Agents
M
### MCP server
Built
Gap: agents learn Pistachio from instructions and shell commands.
Built: pistachio mcp with tools for status, listing items, checking and running a command with references filled in, the checkout's project, writing an env file of references, and asking for a grant. No tool returns a value.
- Agents
M
### Secret requests
Gap: to add a key, an agent has to handle the value or ask you to do it out of band.
Plan: the agent asks for STRIPE_KEY for this project, a notification opens a field in the app, you paste the value, and the agent gets back only the reference.
- AgentsYou
S
### Agent setup kit
Gap: every agent needs to be told how to use Pistachio, and nothing stops it from running cat .env.
Built: the Pistachio skill and Claude Code plugin tell an agent to run through pst run, never print values, and stop on 77 or 66. Next: a hook that blocks commands like cat .env and printenv.
- Agents
L
### Rules beyond one switch
Built
Gap: agent-safe is one yes/no per item.
Built: grants per folder and its worktrees, for a time, until the agent quits, for one command or one request, e.g. pst grant shop/development/DATABASE_URL --command "npm test".
- AgentsYou
L
### Header-injecting proxy
Built
Gap: any value in a process's environment can be printed or written to a file.
Built: pst run --proxy gives the command a placeholder and a local base URL, and adds the real OpenAI or Anthropic key only to requests for the provider's host. Next: more providers.
- Agents
Tier 3
## Day-to-day use
Smaller features that remove friction.
M
### Key files
Built
Gap: tools that want a file path (.p8, .pem, service-account JSON) can't use an environment value.
Plan: GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=pistachio-file://gcp-sa writes a 0600 temporary file and deletes it when the command exits.
- YouAgents
M
### Project commands
Gap: there's no standard way to set up a project or check it in CI.
Built: pistachio check confirms what a run would get without reading values, and pistachio export writes an env file of references from the environment's record. Next: pistachio init and a shell hook.
- YouAgents
M
### Last used, expiry and rotation
Gap: nothing says which tokens are stale, unused or about to expire.
Plan: last-used dates from the log, an expiry date per item, reminders before expiry, and a list of items nothing has read in 90 days.
- You
M
### Items with fields
Gap: AWS and database credentials come in sets that are stored as unrelated items.
Plan: group items such as aws.access_key_id and aws.secret_access_key as one card with fields.
- You
M
### Scan for plain-text secrets
Built
Gap: secrets already sitting in repos and old .env files stay there.
Built: pistachio scan finds env files holding a stored value or one that looks secret, naming file, line and item but never the value, and a pre-commit hook refuses those commits.
- YouAgents
S
### Activity alerts
Gap: denied or unusual reads are only visible if you open Activity.
Plan: notifications for denials and first-time callers, and filters by item, folder and outcome.
- You
Tier 4
## Moving in
Getting existing secrets into Pistachio, and getting them back out safely.
S
### Import from Passwords
Gap: tokens you've saved in the Passwords app can't be read by other apps.
Plan: read a Passwords CSV export (File > Export), pick the entries that are really API tokens, import them, then delete the CSV.
- You
M
### Import from other managers
Gap: secrets in 1Password or Bitwarden have to be copied over one by one.
Plan: importers that use the op and bw command-line tools.
- You
M
### Encrypted backup
Gap: there's no copy of your values outside the keychain, so nothing to restore from if it's lost.
Plan: an export encrypted with a passphrase, and a matching restore.
- You
Tier 5
## Later
Larger work that builds on everything above.
L
### SSH agent with Secure Enclave keys
Gap: SSH keys sit on disk as files.
Plan: keys that can't be exported and ask for Touch ID on each use, also usable for git commit signing. Each Mac gets its own key.
- YouAgents
L
### Approve from iPhone
Gap: when you're away from the Mac, only the Apple Watch can approve.
Plan: an iPhone companion that receives approval requests, for agents working while you're out.
- YouAgents
M
### Distribution
Built: a notarized disk image, a Homebrew cask, and in-app updates for the download.
Plan: release the Mac App Store version, where Pro is sold. Its one-time purchase and restore are built.
- You
M
### Test coverage
Gap: there are no end-to-end tests for pistachio run or the socket server, and no UI tests.
Plan: tests that run the CLI against a broker with a test approver, plus a few UI tests for the window.
- You
## Limits and non-goals
### Items in the Passwords app
Apple doesn't let other apps write to or read from the Passwords app. Pistachio uses the same iCloud Keychain underneath, in its own group. CSV import is the bridge.
### Passkeys as API tokens
A passkey only signs logins for one website. Pistachio uses the same Touch ID check for approvals, and Secure Enclave keys for SSH.
### Teams and other platforms
Pistachio is for one person's Macs. Windows and Linux are out of scope, and shared team vaults would be Pistachio Teams, a separate product.
Sizes are rough. "Built" marks what's done; "Next up" marks the recommended next batch.

Keep your projects, credentials and coding agents working together, with access you can inspect and control. Pistachio is free to download and use, and the core is meant to stay free. Pro will add more for a one-time price in the Mac App Store.
