Page: Security model: what's protected and where it stops · Pistachio
URL: https://latchkey.snackstud.io/security.html

# What Pistachio protects, and where it stops
Pistachio keeps secret values out of files and transcripts, and makes you the one who decides which command gets which value. Every mechanism has a boundary, and the boundaries matter as much as the mechanisms.
- Storage
- Sync
- Who's asking
- Releasing values
- Delivery paths
- The log
- Guarantees
- Limits
- Reporting
A reference in a committed file names the item and nothing more. A script that asks Pistachio directly, instead of through the signed pst tool, is named by its path with a warning, and is refused unless you allow it. The scene uses example data.
## Six distinctions worth knowing
- The keychain protects stored values, not released ones.Once a command has a value, it's in that command's memory and environment, and Pistachio can't control what it does with it: print it, write it to a file or send it on. Masking catches exact copies in output, not changed ones.
- A reference names a secret; it doesn't grant access to it.pistachio://shop/development/STRIPE_KEY in a committed file reveals a name. Reading the item still needs it to be agent-safe, a grant covering the caller, or your approval.
- A proxy hides a key without narrowing what it can do.With --proxy the command never holds the OpenAI or Anthropic key, but it can still make any call that key allows through the proxy. --proxy-models and --proxy-requests narrow that.
- iCloud Keychain sync is separate from agent authorization.Items and environment records sync to your Macs. Grants don't: each is kept on the Mac where you made it.
- The access log records releases, not provider-side use.It shows what Pistachio gave to which program, from where. What that program then did at the service is the service's record.
- A shared credential means fewer copies of the same authority.One shared item used by five projects is one value to rotate, and still one key that all five can use.
## Storage
Values live in the keychain, behind the signed app.
- Values are generic-password items in the data-protection keychain, in an access group only the signed Pistachio app can use. Versions, remote links, environment records and project links are keychain items too; records and links hold item IDs, remotes and plain settings, nothing secret. A plain setting that looks secret is refused.
- One process holds values. The command-line tool never touches the keychain; it asks the app over a Unix socket readable and writable only by you, and the app accepts connections only from your user account.
- Before sending anything, a signed pistachio checks that the program on the socket is the Pistachio app signed by the same team. A program that took the socket while the app wasn't running gets nothing, not even a value you're saving. An unsigned development build can't check, and falls back to the login keychain on one Mac.
- Synced items use the "after first unlock" protection class, so scheduled jobs can read agent-safe items while the screen is locked.
## Sync between Macs
iCloud Keychain carries items; permissions stay put.
Pistachio's items sync through iCloud Keychain, end to end encrypted, to each Mac signed in to your Apple Account that has Pistachio installed. There's no Pistachio server or account. That protection is Apple's: anyone who controls your Apple Account and a trusted device can reach synced items. Apple describes it in iCloud Keychain security overview and iCloud data security overview.
Grants, approvals and the access log stay on each Mac. A second Mac gets your items and environment records, not the permissions you gave agents on the first. Second-Mac test pending
## Who's asking
Identity comes from the kernel, not the request.
- For each connection the app gets the caller's identity from the kernel, not from the request: its working folder, its command line, its parent processes, and whether it is Pistachio's own command-line tool, by code signature.
- The approval panel and the log show those. Any other program talking to the socket is named by its path, with a warning. Grants are matched against the folder the caller really runs in.
- The caller is checked by signature; its parents are named by their files, and file names can be faked. Judge a request by its folder and command as well.
## Releasing values
Approvals, grants, and items agents may read.
### Approvals
Approvals use macOS LocalAuthentication: Touch ID, a paired Apple Watch, or your account password. Every request shows Pistachio's panel with what it covers and the caller's folder, command and process chain, and Touch ID is read inside the panel; Use Password… opens the system sheet. Touch ID runs in the Secure Enclave either way, so a lookalike panel drawn by another app gets a touch that authorizes nothing. Requests from the same process tree in the same folder that arrive while the panel is up are listed in it and answered by one touch, and a request joining restarts Touch ID. Pushes, requests over SSH, from Pistachio for Safari or from a program that isn't identified are always asked on their own. Nothing unanswered is allowed: a request is denied after two minutes. Allow Once authorizes one request; approvals are never cached.
A request doesn't hold Pistachio while it waits for you. When you answer, it runs again from the start and uses your answer only if it asks the same thing about values that haven't changed; otherwise it asks again.
### App lock
Pistachio's window, Settings and menu bar panel lock behind Touch ID (in the lock screen or the menu bar panel itself) or your Mac password when it opens, after time in the background and when the Mac sleeps or the screen locks, and revealed values are hidden. The lock keeps the window private; it doesn't decide what's released. Requests from commands, agents and Safari still go through approval, locked or not.
### Grants
A grant lets commands from one folder (and its repository's worktrees) read named items without asking, for as long as the approval says (any length of time, or until you revoke it), and can be narrowed to an agent's session, one command or one request. Grants are kept in a keychain item only Pistachio can read or change, on this Mac only. No file holds them, so no other program can write itself one. Grants an agent asks for through the MCP server cover only its own folder, end with the agent's session, and can't include production.
### Agent-safe items
An item marked agent-safe is released to any program that asks, with no prompt. Use it for values that aren't really secret, such as NEXT_PUBLIC_* settings that ship to browsers anyway.
## How a command gets a value
The guarantee depends on which path a value takes into the command.
PathWhat the command holdsWhat it protects
pst runThe value, in its environmentFiles and transcripts hold references; output that repeats an exact value of 6 characters or more is masked.
--proxyA random placeholder and a base URL on 127.0.0.1The OpenAI or Anthropic key stays in the signed pst process and goes only to the provider's own host. Requests without that run's placeholder are refused; upstream redirects aren't followed.
--aws-sessionSTS credentials that expire (15 minutes by default)The long-lived AWS key stays in pst run. A leaked value soon stops working.
--fileThe path of a temporary fileThe file is in a new folder only you can open, readable only by you, and deleted when the command exits.
export --valuesA plain-text fileAsks every time, naming the file; nothing stands in for that approval. Written readable only by you and renamed into place. Agents can't use it.
## Pistachio for Safari
Sandboxed, and limited to names, saves and one fill.
The extension is sandboxed and reaches the app through its own socket, which admits only Pistachio's signed extension and only to list item names, save a value (which asks like any change) and fill one item into the page you're on. Key detection runs inside the page: a value goes to the app only when you press Save. Password fields aren't read. Fill asks every time, works only on the item's fill sites (by default its service's own site and deployment platforms), over https only, never in a frame, and is logged. Otherwise it can't read a stored value.
## The access log
Every read, change, grant, move, import and push is logged with the program chain and folder. Stored values aren't logged; likely secrets in command arguments are replaced with <redacted>, which is heuristic, so keep values out of command arguments. Each entry carries a keyed hash (HMAC-SHA256) of itself and the one before it, with the key kept in the keychain, so pst log --verify finds an entry that was changed, removed or added, or a log cut short. It can't stop a program running as you from deleting the file, only show that it happened.
## Guarantees and limits
Each mechanism, what it protects against, and what it doesn't promise.
MechanismProtects againstDoesn't guarantee
Keychain storageValues in plaintext files, backups and synced folders; values readable on a lost MacSafety after a value is released to a command
ReferencesSecrets copied into config files and commitsPermission to read the item
Approval panelReads you didn't approve; shows the caller as macOS sees itControl over what an approved command does next
GrantsRepeated prompts for a folder, for a timeTelling programs apart within that folder: any program asking from there is covered
MaskingExact copies of a value in a command's outputCatching values that were encoded or transformed
Key proxyThe OpenAI or Anthropic key reaching the commandLimits on which calls the command makes with it; protection for other credentials
STS credentialsThe long-lived AWS key reaching the commandLeast privilege, which depends on the role's policy
Access logUndetected edits, removals or truncationA record of what the service saw, or protection against the file being deleted
iCloud KeychainValues exposed in transit or at rest between your MacsSafety from someone with your Apple Account and a trusted device
Shared itemsMany copies of the same valueSeparate authority per project
## Where protection ends
Read these before you rely on Pistachio.
- Anything running as you can ask. The socket is open to every process in your user account. Agent-safe items and grants are released to any program that asks from the right place, so keep them narrow and short.
- A released value is out of Pistachio's hands. A command can write it to a file, send it over the network or transform it. Masking only hides exact copies.
- pst get prints the value. Keep agents away from it with your agent instructions or a hook that refuses it.
- The same Mac account. Malware running as you could ask for approvals until you click one, or read a temporary key file while the command runs. Pistachio raises the bar; it doesn't replace a clean machine.
- History keeps old values for up to 30 days after deletion, or until there are more than 10 versions. Use Forget History when an old value shouldn't linger, and rotate leaked keys at the service either way.
- An exported file is a plain copy. Delete it when you're done, and keep it out of Git.
The full write-up is in the repository's docs/security.md, with the wire protocol and stored files described under References and API.
## Reporting a problem
Privately, never in public.
Report a vulnerability privately: by email to Contact support with "Security" in the subject, or through GitHub, in the repository's Security tab › Report a vulnerability. Please don't open a public issue for it. Include the Pistachio and macOS versions, what an attacker can do and what they need first, and steps to reproduce with example values only. Never send a real secret.
## Stop being the credential courier.
Keep your projects, credentials and coding agents working together, with access you can inspect and control. Pistachio is free to download and use, and the core is meant to stay free. Pro will add more for a one-time price in the Mac App Store.
Download freeSee what Pro adds

# Support and troubleshooting
Most answers are in the docs. For anything else, write to Contact support; we answer by email.
## Start here
- Quickstart: install, import an env file and run a command.
- The command-line tool: getting it with the Mac App Store version or the direct download.
- CLI reference and Agents and MCP.
- pistachio status shows whether the command-line tool reaches the app, how you approve, and where values are kept. Include its output when you write (it never shows values).
## Common problems
- "cannot reach the Pistachio app" (exit 69): the tool starts Pistachio itself, so this usually means PISTACHIO_NO_LAUNCH=1 is set or the app can't start. Open Pistachio (the current download) once and try again. It stays in the menu bar after you close its window, and keeps answering the tool.
- A command still sees pistachio:// references: run it through pst run -- …, which replaces them with values for that command only.
- Values don't appear on another Mac: both Macs need iCloud Keychain turned on with the same Apple Account, and the items must have been saved to iCloud Keychain. Syncing to a second Mac hasn't been tested end to end yet.
## Pistachio Pro
Pro isn't on sale yet. When it is, it's bought in the Mac App Store. To unlock it on another Mac, sign in with the same Apple Account and choose Restore Purchases in Pistachio's Settings. Refunds go through Apple at reportaproblem.apple.com.
## Report a mistake on this site
If a page says something Pistachio doesn't do, or leaves out a limit, email Contact support with the page and what's wrong, or open an issue. Corrections are listed in the changelog.
## Report a security issue
Please don't post it publicly. Email Contact support with "Security" in the subject, the Pistachio and macOS versions, what an attacker can do and what they need first, and steps to reproduce with example values only. Never send a real secret. Security explains what's in scope.
## More
Privacy policy · Terms · Roadmap

# Developer Credential Migration
We help a small development team find every env file it depends on, see which credentials are duplicated, stale or in conflict, and move its supported local workflows into Pistachio, with safer access for its coding agents.
From $2,500per small-team engagement · fixed scope
Request an assessmentWhat's included
Requests go to latchkey@snackstud.io. Scope, confidentiality and credential handling are agreed in writing before any work starts.
The inventory starts with a dry run that prints names and counts, never values: where each file goes, the key every project shares, what expires, and files that disagree. Example data; the output is what Pistachio prints.
## What the engagement leaves you with
A result, not a license: your team's credentials organized, its Macs set up, and the procedures written down.
- Credential and environment inventoryEvery env file under your projects, where each value would go, and what's shared, skipped or in conflict.
- Dependency and migration reportWhich projects and environments use which credentials, the duplicates and stale ones, and the order to move them in.
- Pistachio set up on supported MacsProjects linked to their repositories, env files of references, and environment records your developers can export on any Mac.
- Access and recovery proceduresHow each developer gets a credential, what agents may read without asking, how grants are made, and how to rotate and restore.
- Onboarding and handoffA walkthrough for your developers, and the documentation to bring the next one on without us.
- Safer agent accessGrants scoped to folders, sessions and commands, and the agent instructions that keep values out of transcripts.
## How it runs
- 1Agree scopeWhich projects, Macs and deployment platforms, and how credentials are handled, in writing.
- 2InventoryDry runs on your team's Macs: names, counts, duplicates and conflicts, never values.
- 3MigrateImports with one approval per developer, references in place of values, projects and records set up.
- 4Hand offProcedures, onboarding, and a check that every project runs through Pistachio.
## How your credentials are handled
- Values are stored in each developer's iCloud Keychain, not on a Snack Studio server; the inventory and reports work from names and counts, which is all pst import --dry-run prints.
- Each import and grant is approved by the developer whose Mac it is, with Touch ID.
- Scope, confidentiality and credential-handling terms are agreed in writing before we start. We don't accept customer secrets outside those terms.
A dry run lists names, never values; the import asks the developer whose Mac it is for Touch ID, and leaves references in the file. Example data; the output is what Pistachio prints.
## What it covers, and what it doesn't
Fixed scope, limited to what Pistachio supports today.
- Covered: Macs on macOS 15 or later, env files and the local workflows Pistachio supports, and linking environments to Vercel, GitHub Actions, Railway or Fly.
- Not covered: Windows or Linux machines, secrets platforms already in production use that we'd have to replace, or a security audit. It's an implementation engagement, not security consulting.
- Pricing starts at $2,500 for a small team; larger scopes are quoted before the work is agreed.
Pistachio Teams · in design
## Shared environments for the whole team
Pistachio, and Pistachio Pro after it, are for one developer's Macs. Teams would be a separate product for what organizations automating development ask for:
- Shared organizational environments and managed team credentials
- Membership, roles and team provisioning
- Approval workflows and central evidence of access
$15 per user a month, billed yearly, planned
We'll build it with two or three teams who would pay for it, before building a hosted service. If your team wants shared environments, organizational controls and audit evidence, we'd like to hear what it would need to do.
Become a design partner
In design. Write to latchkey@snackstud.io to be one of the first two or three teams.

# Terms of use
Pistachio is made by Snack Studio. These terms cover the app, its command-line tool, MCP server and Safari extension, and this website.
Effective 12 November 2026.
## Which terms apply
- Copies from the Mac App Store, including Pistachio Pro, are licensed under Apple's Licensed Application End User License Agreement, together with these terms.
- The direct download is free to use under these terms.
- The source code is licensed under the Functional Source License, Version 1.1, ALv2 Future License (FSL-1.1-ALv2). Each version becomes available under the Apache License 2.0 two years after it's released.
## Pistachio Pro
Pro isn't on sale yet. When it is:
- Pro is a one-time in-app purchase in the Mac App Store version. It unlocks Pro features on the Macs signed in to your Apple Account, under Apple's rules for purchases and Family Sharing.
- Pro includes the Pro features described on the pricing page and the updates we release to them. There's no subscription.
- Apple handles payment, receipts and refunds. To ask for a refund, use reportaproblem.apple.com.
- Storing, reading and exporting your own values never depends on Pro, and stays available if Pro is ever unavailable.
## Your credentials and your responsibility
- Your values are yours. Pistachio keeps them in your keychain; Snack Studio never has access to them.
- You're responsible for what you approve: a command, agent or platform you allow receives the values you give it. Security explains what each protection does and where it ends.
- Keep your own backups and recovery: if you lose access to your Apple Account and devices, we can't recover your values.
## Acceptable use
Don't use Pistachio to get at credentials you aren't authorized to use, or to break the terms of the platforms you connect it to.
## No warranty
Pistachio is provided "as is", without warranties of any kind, to the extent the law allows. To the extent the law allows, Snack Studio isn't liable for indirect or consequential losses, or for losses from credentials you released, exported or pushed, and its total liability is limited to what you paid for Pistachio. Nothing here limits rights you have under the law where you live that can't be limited.
